entry.title: Klimt’s The Kiss and the Home Alone House: The Best LEGO Sets for Adults
entry.summary: From a beginner-friendly hanging pothos plant to a highly anticipated Godzilla.
entry.content:
Whether they’ve been obsessed with LEGO since childhood or picked up the hobby more recently, choosing the perfect set for an AFOL — a.k.a. an adult fan of LEGO — can be a bit overwhelming. So I asked four adult LEGO enthusiasts for their recommendations on how to shop and which sets might be on your recipient’s wish list this year.

According to Dan Zarzo, a LEGO fan creator and half of the duo behind @twogayafols, it is best to start with your giftee’s interests: “As soon as there is a theme that you’re passionate about, it doesn’t matter the difficulty of the set — you’ll enjoy it,” he says. And there truly is a LEGO set for every interest, from Formula 1 to Downton Abbey. “One of the coolest parts about LEGO and the reason it’s such a versatile gift is that you don’t have to be a LEGO fan,” adds LEGO fan creator Colin Wylie. Just about anyone can appreciate a themed LEGO set as a piece of pop-culture memorabilia or a representation of some part of their life, even if they aren’t a regular builder.

Of course, you’ll also want to consider the size of the set, how easy or difficult it is to build, and your own gift budget. “If the person is in a small New York apartment, you probably shouldn’t get them a humungous LEGO set,” Wylie says, unless you know for sure they want a major display piece. Generally, larger sets are also more expensive and take longer to build. As far as complexity goes, the age range printed on the box is more of a rough guideline than a hard-and-fast rule: “Just because it says 8-plus doesn’t mean it’s for kids necessarily,” says LEGO fan creator Jamie Rhodes, though those sets will skew more approachable. “If it says 16- or 18-plus, those are probably more advanced builds,” but that doesn’t mean they are too involved for tweens or younger teens to complete, Rhodes says.

The experience of building can also vary by set — some are more repetitive than others, says LEGO fan creator Giavanna Paradiso. LEGO’s Architecture line, for example, is known for having lots of repetition; while Paradiso finds that meditative, others prefer builds with more variation.

And finally, while you can definitely splash out on LEGO sets that cost hundreds of dollars, the fans I spoke to emphasized thlat in the world of LEGO, more expensive doesn’t always translate to better and that you can get just as much enjoyment out of smaller, cheaper sets.

All the LEGO fans I spoke with brought up the Botanicals line as especially gift-worthy. Paradiso says many people who’ve recently gotten into LEGO started with Botanicals because the sets tend to be smaller and simpler to build.

They make nice displays without taking up too much space. “You can go from a very little set with, like, three or four flowers to the big bouquets that are more technical to build, but they’re still easy,” says Zarzo. You can also give multiple sets if they might want to create a bigger floral display.

Here’s a more woodsy take on the Botanicals theme: a tree stump sprouting with fiber cap, earthstar, chanterelle, bonnet, and other types of mushrooms.

This LEGO bonsai comes with green leaves and pink blossoms to change with the seasons.

“Speed Champions is a car line, and they’re all smaller model cars,” Wylie says. “They may be a little more technical, but the size makes it a lot more manageable, where the average person could probably knock it out in an hour to an hour and a half.”

Paradiso says the LEGO postcards are among the most underrated sets, especially for gift-giving, because they are very affordable and make excellent display pieces. “My cousin just got married in Italy over the summer, and I got them an Italy postcard because it’s simple to build — it’s under 300 pieces, so it’s not intimidating — and also it’s going to mean something to them,” she says.

This giant replica of the Eiffel Tower is one of Paradiso’s favorite sets, though she notes it is a repetitive build. Standing at almost five feet, it’s the tallest LEGO set ever made.

Some builders, including Paradiso, collect many sets over time to build up their own “LEGO cities.” The official LEGO City theme includes a variety of buildings and vehicles, like this old-school trolley that takes vacationers to the beach.

Zarzo also recommends checking out the LEGO Friends line for other sets with buildings. Though it’s geared toward young girls, Zarzo says it’s equally fun for adults who like the poppy, colorful aesthetic.

The ultimate treehouse, complete with a functional pulley elevator and slide.

Every LEGO fan I spoke to recommended the brand’s art-inspired sets as excellent (though expensive) gifts. They generally don’t take up shelf space since the frames can hang on the wall like real art, and they appeal to a broad audience. Gustav Klimt’s The Kiss, a recent release, is particularly noteworthy.

Monet’s famous water lilies also got the LEGO treatment this year and have been quite popular, according to Zarzo. He says LEGO art sets can be especially fun to build because they often reuse established pieces — a fork, a sword, a butterfly — to create the different objects and textures in each artwork. For example, this set uses Ninjago swords to make tall grass along the pond.

This is Paradiso’s all-time favorite LEGO set because of the striking colors and mosaic-style image.

Over the years, LEGO has released hundreds of sets based on movies, TV shows, and video games. There are dozens of very cool and intricate Harry Potter sets covering just about every aspect of the franchise, but this one based on The Sorcerer’s Stone came out quite recently and would make a great collector’s piece.

Since this is the first Spongebob SquarePants set LEGO has released in several years, Wylie anticipates it will be especially popular this holiday season.

LEGO and Pokémon collaborated for the first time earlier year, so this set with three classic Pokémon has also been highly sought-after.

But if you aren’t looking to spend quite so much, there are some some excellent more affordable Pokémon releases as well.

Every set from the LEGO Ideas collection is based on fan submissions, like this recent The X-Files set, which was a decade in the making.

The first-ever LEGO Peanuts set also came out this year.

If they’re settling in for a Downton Abbey rewatch, give them this detailed replica of Highclere Castle, which inspired the show. Multiple LEGO fans I spoke to mentioned this as one that’s likely on many people’s wish lists (or on their own).

Paradiso says all her LEGO friends have been obsessed with this set replicating the Elven valley from The Lord of the Rings. There are also sets based on the Shire, Minas Tirith, and Barad-dûr that will appeal to fans of the series.

Every year, LEGO launches a highly anticipated pop-culture set for Black Friday. This Star Trek set — LEGO’s first Star Trek set — was the 2025 Black Friday release.

And this year’s is Godzilla, which Wylie says is sure to be very popular. It will officially become available on November 27.

Wylie described this Death Star set as the ultimate display piece for a Star Wars fan. It’s also the most expensive LEGO set to date.

LEGO Technic is a line of LEGO sets that uses slightly different styles of pieces than the traditional bricks and is geared more toward adults who want to build something complex. According to Wylie, nearly everything outside of the Technic line can be pretty beginner-friendly, but Technic sets are challenging enough that he wouldn’t give one to a total newbie. They would, however, make a fantastic gift for experienced LEGO fans seeking a challenge.

“Every LEGO set has a shelf life. They can’t be on shelves forever or else they wouldn’t have space for new products,” Wylie says. On the LEGO website, sets that are due to retire at the end of the year will be marked as “Retiring Soon,” like this LEGO Ideas Polaroid OneStep SX-70 Camera. You can actually load “film” into the final build and eject it by pressing the red button.

Wylie advises that if you know your recipient wants a retiring set — like this retro arcade game that opens to reveal a gamer lounge and mini-figure — don’t wait to buy it, as it could potentially sell out and will only become more expensive at third-party retailers once it’s officially retired. Rhodes says soon-to-retire sets also make great gifts because of the potential resale value. If your recipient ends up moving or needing to make space later, there’s a good chance they can resell the set down the road.

LEGO releases one new addition to its Winter Village every year; this year’s is a festively decorated house and horse-drawn sleigh.

entry.title: The 7 Very Best Portable Chargers
entry.summary: For extra power when you need it.
entry.content:
Whether you’re trying to get through one more Zoom meeting from the park or trying to hail an Uber at 2 a.m., you want to make sure your phone and laptop is charged — and that’s where a capable, reliable portable power bank comes in.

The best portable charger for your needs has plenty of capacity to keep your devices charged (or even charge them multiple times), the ability to do that quickly, and enough ports to handle everything you need to keep alive. High-capacity power banks can power a laptop and charge your device several times, but they are big and expensive, while ultracompact chargers fit into a pocket with just enough capacity to top up a phone.

One thing that’s certain about choosing a portable charger is that you want to know where it comes from so you don’t fry your phone. You can find tons of battery packs from unknown brands on Amazon, but I would recommend choosing a brand that has a yearslong reputation for building reliable products that last. (This is a category in which it matters — you don’t want to risk a no-name device that may overheat or worse.) Anker is one of the best-known brands, but companies like Belkin, Mophie, BioLite, EcoFlow, Nitecore, and Moft also make good chargers.

To find the best options, I tested more than 30 power banks and portable chargers while going about my days.

Updated on November 24, 2026
All our picks are in stock and we’ve confirmed that prices are up-to-date.

A portable charger should have at least one USB-C port to plug a cable into, but we looked for chargers with extra ports, built-in cables, or wireless charging via Qi 2 and MagSafe. Those additions typically impact the shape of the charger. A device that prioritizes wireless charging will have to be compact enough to fit on the back of a phone, and one with built-in cables needs enough room to store the cables when they are not in use. Keep in mind that wireless charging is slower and less efficient than hooking up a cable, and it can overheat your phone if left attached for too long. For compatibility with older cables and gear you’ll want to look for portable chargers with USB-A ports (though most companies have abandoned them in favor of USB-C ports, which are more modern and allow for a slimmer design).

Many power banks have a capacity of at least 5,000 milliamp hours (mAh). That’s barely enough to charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max (which has a capacity of 5,088 mAh) one time. If you want one that’ll charge your phone more than once, a portable charger with 10,000 mAh is a better choice. Some power banks can even recharge a laptop, though you’ll have to double check your laptop’s battery capacity (an M1 MacBook Pro has roughly 5,152 mAh) as well as its wattage requirements (see below) to make sure it can give you a full recharge.

Charging speed is determined not only by the charger output, but also by the charging rate the device (and charging cable) can accept. For a phone, a power bank that delivers 18W or more is considered fast-charging, meaning you can get your smart phone from 0 to 50 percent in about half an hour (though this may not be true in very hot or very cold environments). Laptops require 60 to 80W for charging, so be sure to look out for chargers with faster speeds if your laptop frequently needs recharging.

I also considered the method by which you actually charge the power bank; every one I recommend can be charged using a USB-C cable, but most will require you to carry a power brick with you to recharge it. Some chargers, however, have built-in A/C plugs so you can plug it directly into the wall like a regular charging brick and refuel while your phone is charging — and usually at a higher speed to boot.

A heavy portable charger isn’t truly portable, so for chargers meant for phones and other mobile devices, I only considered options that weighed around half a pound or less. For higher-capacity laptop chargers, I considered ones that weigh just over a pound, but only if they could charge a laptop at least twice.

Power banks with pass-through charging are able to charge other devices while being charged themselves. This is particularly handy when traveling. You can charge both your power bank and phone overnight using a single outlet (and if you get one with multiple outlets, you don’t have to pack a power strip and charger for work trips).

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C port (1); built-in USB-C cable (2) | Capacity: 10,000 mAh | Charging speed: 30W | Weight: 0.55 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

While many brands use labels like “Signature Series” to charge a premium for devices with negligible benefits over the regular model, Mophie’s fancy line of chargers features genuine improvements with an attention to detail you’d expect of a flagship product. The body of the Powerstation Plus 10k is made of soft-touch plastic that’s quite pleasant and secure to handle compared with the cheaper-feeling plastic of the BoostCharge Plus, with borders that give the charger a refined metallic look. I’ve dropped it a couple times, and it still looks new.

The Powerstation has a single USB-C port that supports fast charging up to 30 watts, but there are also two built-in cables that save you the trouble of carrying extra charging cables. They’re made from a braided fabric that’s tougher and more elegant than the Belkin’s rubber-coated cables. When not in use, the cables are held in place by magnets on the connectors, which provide a satisfying click that’s both secure and makes the device a worthy fidget toy. Handy as they are, the cables are quite short, so you can’t keep this in your back pocket and charge your phone unless you use an additional cable. If you’re on the go, you’ll want to keep your phone charging in a jacket pocket or bag.

With a 10,000 mAh capacity, the Powerstation can charge an iPhone 17 Pro twice with a bit of juice to spare. If you need to charge multiple devices at once, you can use both built-in cables and the USB-C port to charge up to three devices simultaneously.

My only complaint: The Powerstation’s soft-touch finish is an absolute fingerprint magnet. If you have oily fingers, you’ll likely need to wipe this charger down after you’re done using it. Even so, the overall premium feel of the Mophie’s materials makes up for that inconvenience. It isn’t enough to detract from how nice it looks.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C port (1); built-in USB-C cable (1); built-in Lightning cable (1) | Capacity: 10,000 mAh | Charging speed: 23W | Weight: 0.66 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

If you have an old iPhone with a Lightning connector that’s always in need of a boost or just want to spend a little less, Belkin’s Boostcharge Plus 10k offers nearly all the same core features as the Powerstation Plus — with just a bit less polish. It’s slightly taller and a tad thinner than the Mophie, but its textured plastic shell isn’t as nice to touch.

Like the Mophie, this charger has two built-in cables: one USB-C and an antiquated (backward-compatible) Lightning cable for older Apple devices. Both are coated in a rubbery material that lacks the elegance of the Mophie’s braided cables. Additionally, they require more guidance to be placed back into their slots when not in use. You have to drag your finger down the cable to get each piece in place, whereas the Mophie’s cables just snap right back.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C port (2); USB-A port (1); detachable USB-C cable (1) | Capacity: 10,000 mAh | Charging speed: 45W | Weight: 0.35 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

INIU’s Pocket Rocket is as practical as it is charming. Its footprint is smaller than a credit card’s — though it’s about as thick as a deck of playing cards — and it can easily fit in a small pocket. There are three ports: two USB-C ports and one USB-A. Unlike the Powerstation or Boostcharge, it doesn’t technically have a built-in cable, but it does come with a detachable USB-C to USB-C one that acts as a loop you can hook onto a carabiner or keychain when not in use.

While the Mophie and Belkin both use four-dot indicators to give a rough estimate of how much power they have, the Pocket Rocket has an alphanumeric display that shows an accurate percentage. That makes it a bit easier to determine whether you can give your device a full boost, and the screen’s frosted finish is nicer to look at.

The Pocket Rocket comes in an assortment of fun colors, including black, white, light green, light blue, light pink, and light purple.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C (1); USB-A (1); MagSafe and Qi 2 | Capacity: 10,000 mAh | Charging speed: 7.5W (wireless), 20W (wired)| Weight: 0.48 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

For charging my phone on the go without a cable, I like Anker’s 633 magnetic charger. It has the polish of Mophie’s Powerstation (without the built-in cables) and has a kickstand to hold your phone up for hands-free viewing. In addition to wireless charging, the 633 has one USB-C port and one USB-A port in case you’re clinging to some old cables. Using all three allows you to charge three devices simultaneously. The wattage does vary, however, for each method. The USB-A port maxes out at 18 watts, the USB-C port can charge up to 20 watts, while the wireless charging pad is limited to just 7.5 watts. That means it’s not as fast as some other wireless chargers (such as the Mophie Powerstation), but it’s quick enough to give your phone a boost in times of need. The magnets are quite strong, so it’ll stay attached to your phone.

It’s a nice addition, but I wish the Anker’s kickstand were as sturdy and adjustable as the Mophie’s Powerstation Wireless Stand. The 633’s kickstand folds out vertically (just like the Mophie’s) and can be positioned at nearly any angle, but it’s made from a thinner metal that doesn’t stay as firmly in place. The stand itself isn’t too wobbly, but I’m more worried about its longevity than the Mophie’s. And for the nitpickers, it’s worth noting that when attached to the back of my iPhone 17 Pro without a case, the 633 hung just below my iPhone’s lip. You won’t notice this unless you use your phone while it’s charging, but once you see it, you can’t unsee it, and if you’re picky — but not picky enough to have your phone in a case — you may find it unseemly.

Like our overall best portable charger, Mophie’s more expensive Powerstation Wireless Stand has a polished look and feel, and it feels a lot fancier than Anker’s 633. It’s made of an anodized aluminum rather than the Anker’s soft-touch plastic, and its kickstand is both nicer to use and more functional. The stand can be propped up at any angle just like the 633’s, but this one can also rotate to four different positions (think of a cross), so you can use it horizontally or vertically. I also like that it features a fabric finish, and that Mophie cleverly hid all the ugly logos and technical jargon on the back of the stand so you never see it.

Handy as wireless chargers are, they’re often quite bulky. Not so with Anker’s incredibly thin Nano Power Bank, which is only 0.34-inches thick. It has half the capacity of the Anker 633 —enough to charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max from 0 back to 100, but it also won’t be as noticeable in your pocket. If all you need is something to make sure your phone makes it to 2 a.m. when you need to call a Lyft, you’ll be grateful for the Nano’s portability.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C (2) | Capacity: 10,000 mAh | Charging speed: 30W (unplugged) | Weight: 0.31 pounds | Passthrough charging: No

If you want something with a built-in A/C plug so you don’t have to carry a separate power brick, get the Nano 3-in-1, which has a fold-out A/C plug so it can go directly into an outlet. The on-device USB-C cable is longer than the Belkin’s, so it’s easier to use your device while it’s plugged in. There’s also one USB-C port that you can use to plug in another cable and charge two devices at once.

At the top of the charger is a small metal loop that holds the tip of the cable in place when you’re not using it, and while it’s clever, I do wish there was some sort of built-in wrap or other management system so the cable doesn’t just dangle when it’s not plugged in, as that leaves it more vulnerable to damage. And since the cable isn’t replaceable, you’ll have to get a whole new charger if it ever breaks.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C (1), USB-A (1), Built-in USB-C cable (1) | Capacity: 27,000 mAh | Charging speed: 140W | Weight: 1.3 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

For those who need to work or play on the go and frequently run their laptops down to zero percent without an outlet nearby, Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro has enough power to bring it back to 100. Because its capacity is nearly triple that of chargers like the Mophie Powerstation, it’s noticeably larger and heavier, but it won’t weigh your bag down too much. Its plastic shell feels like somewhere between the Boostcharge and the Powerstation; it doesn’t feel cheap, but it’s not particularly fancy either. Like our best portable charger overall, this one has a built-in cable that’s coated in a durable braided material. It’s longer than that of the Mophie, so you can plug it into your laptop while it’s in a backpack and it should reach — I tested it with five backpacks and it worked with each one.

With a capacity of 27,000 mAh, it has enough juice to recharge a MacBook Air or Neo multiple times. And just to be sure, there’s a display on the front to tell you how much charge is left on the battery pack itself. There’s even a fun animation that fills the edge of the screen with a green line to coincide with the percentage — if it’s at 50 percent, the line will cover half of the screen’s edge.

Although it has a slightly lower capacity than the UltraCharge, and it doesn’t have a built-in cable, the BioLite Charge 100 Max can charge a total of five devices at a time. That’s more than any other charger we’ve recommended, and it is perfectly suited for scenarios where multiple people need a boost, like a party or camping trip (its outdoorsy aesthetic certainly doesn’t hurt). It has three USB-C ports, one USB-A port, and a Qi 2 charging pad, though they can’t all charge at the same speed. Two of the USB-C ports cap out at 100W for laptops and tablets, while the third only goes up to 15W, as do the USB-A port and wireless charging pad, meaning those are best reserved for phones and other smaller devices.

Ports and wireless charging: USB-C (1); Qi 2/MagSafe | Capacity: 2,300 mAh | Charging speed: 5W | Charging input: USB-C | Weight: 0.39 pounds | Passthrough charging: Yes

While this shouldn’t be your primary charger if your phone regularly sits at 15 percent, the Clicks Power Keyboard has a retro charm that’s hard to resist. It also makes you more productive when you use your phone. Unlike most portable chargers, which serve the single purpose of bringing your phone’s battery back to an acceptable percentage, the Clicks has a slide-out hardware keyboard that turns your phone into a faux Blackberry. The keys are clicky without being stiff — crucial for long typing sessions — and the customizable shortcuts allow you to do things like open a specific note in your Notes app with just a few keystrokes.

Since it has a capacity of just 2,300 mAh, it’s best not to rely on this one to regularly keep your phone alive (that’s less than the capacity of an iPhone 17 or 18’s battery), but it’s enough to get your phone through a long day. And while it’s not as slim or light as the Nano, it’s light enough to fit in a jean pocket when not in use, so you’ll always have a keyboard handy.

entry.title: The Best Tablets
entry.summary: The best iPads and Android and Amazon Fire tablets for productivity, gaming, reading, and everything else.
entry.content:
A tablet, these days, can be anything you want it to be. You can dedicate it to reading, watching movies, or gaming; tap and swipe your way around for work or play; or even connect it to an external display, keyboard, and mouse and use it in place of a laptop — which is what I do day to day.

Over the course of several weeks, I’ve been putting multiple tablets through their paces to figure out which one is the best for different scenarios. If you’re a pro who wants a tablet to work on, I got you. If you just need one to keep your kid entertained with educational apps, I got you, too. What if you just want the best overall tablet? Don’t worry — I got you.

Updated on November 24, 2026
We’ve added Amazon’s new Alexa Tablet and Kids Tablet in place of their discontinued Fire tablet predecessors, along with the new iPad Mini, and we have checked pricing and confirmed availability for our other recommendations.

There aren’t many operating systems to choose from when it comes to tablets: Apple’s iPadOS or Google’s Android (Amazon’s tablets now run Android with some customizations following the discontinuation of Fire OS). Each one has its pros and cons in terms of interaction, but its largely a matter of what you prefer. Overall app availability is heavily reliant on the operating system, with iPadOS leading the way in overall quality and selection, though Android tablet app support has largely caught up.

If you’re thinking of a tablet as a general-purpose replacement for a computer, keeping it in the family when you choose a tablet can let you share accounts and apps easily with your other devices, so if you’re using mostly Apple products, for instance, an iPad might be the way to go.

Tablets are available with screens ranging from seven to 13 inches. Smaller screens make for a more portable device that’s easier to hold in the hand while reading books or watching videos while traveling; larger screens allow for multitasking and other laptoplike tasks, from gaming to editing photos or video.

If you’re going to be using the tablet primarily for browsing the web, reading books, checking email, and watching the occasional video, then you’d be fine with a lower-resolution display. However, if you’re going to be using your tablet as your main computer, especially if you need it to edit photos and video, then a higher-quality display is something to consider.

The amount of storage you need depends on what you’ll be using the tablet for, of course, but for most people 256GB is a good starting point if you’re planning to download lots of apps, games, and videos. For e-readers, even 16GB of storage is more than enough to store thousands of books.

Most tablets come with a minimum of 128GB of storage, and you’ll find capacities up to 2TB in some powerful models meant to replace a laptop. Amazon’s tablets are available with smaller amounts of memory, starting at 64GB. If you need occasional access to more storage, you can use external storage devices over USB-C.

Battery life for nearly all tablets ranges from ten to 18 hours of continuous use (battery life is typically measured while continually either watching videos or browsing the web). Longer battery life is something I think we can all agree is a good thing, but any tablet will get you through the day even if you’re a heavy user. Unless you live on your tablet, the current battery-life standard among tablets is more than likely good enough.

All of the tablets we looked at connect over Wi-Fi; for many, 5G cellular is available as an option if you’re interested in a stand-alone workstation or just want to be able to connect on the go without having to tether to a phone.

Operating system: iPadOS | Display: 11-inch (2,360 x 1,640) | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 10 hours | Cellular: Optional 5G

It’s crazy to think Apple’s released 11 generations of the base iPad, and it’s still setting the standard for all tablets. Apple — routinely refining the overall design and software each year — still provides the best all-around tablet experience, especially when you consider the affordable price tag of the entry-level model.

The base iPad — which does just about everything you might need from a tablet — is available in four fun colors: silver, blue, pink, and yellow. It’s equipped with an 11-inch, 2,360-by-1,640-pixel display that’s big and sharp enough for bingeing the latest Netflix documentary or catching up on your Facebook feed and emails.

It’s available with 128GB, 256GB, or 512GB of storage, and if you plan on using it on the go often, you can even opt for a 5G-equipped model for constant connectivity.

With ten hours of battery life, you’re able to watch a movie or two on a cross-country flight, or keep the kids entertained with extended gaming sessions. That said, if you regularly face long-haul travel, you’ll want to take along a USB-C battery pack: It doesn’t come close to the 18-hour battery life of Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S11.

Even when using iPadOS 26’s multitasking feature, which enables the use of multiple apps, in smaller windows, at the same time, the iPad’s Apple A16 processor is more than capable of handling everything I ask of it. I routinely have a YouTube video streaming in picture-in-picture mode, with Safari, Mail, Slack, and Ivory open, and I bounce between each window without any performance hiccups. It does feel a bit cramped compared to the iPad Pro’s larger 13-inch display, though.

If you’re planning on doing a lot of typing or want to use the tablet for taking notes, it supports Apple’s Magic Keyboard Folio as well as the vast majority of Bluetooth keyboards and both the first-generation Apple Pencil and the newer Apple Pencil (USB-C), if you’re interested in drawing or handwritten note-taking.

Operating system: Android | Display: 11-inch AMOLED 2X (2,560 x 1,600) | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB | External storage: microSD up to 2TB, USB-C | Battery life: 18 hours | Cellular: None

Samsung’s Galaxy Tab lineup has gotten pretty good in recent years as Samsung has continued to improve and add to the overall Android tablet experience with its own software tweaks, while packing its tablets full of the latest tech that, in many ways, outpaces Apple’s iPad lineup.

What makes the Tab S11 the best Android tablet is Samsung’s own software tweaks to improve upon the tablet experience, specifically DeX (Desktop eXperience), which lets you multitask as you would on a computer by resizing app windows, placing them anywhere on the screen, and using up to five at the same time instead of simply being stuck with Android phone apps that are stretched across the screen. Apple has since introduced multiple app windows with iPadOS 26, but DeX goes much further — you can set up multiple workspaces with different apps or even hook up an external monitor to your Tab and use it as the heart of a desktop system, something you can’t really do with an iPad.

The Tab S11 boasts an 11-inch display with a slightly higher resolution than the standard iPad, at 2,560 by 1,600. However, instead of an LED display, the S11 is equipped with an Amoled 2X display that’s up to three times brighter than the iPad’s screen and features more saturated colors.

The best part about the S11 is how thin it feels. It’s only 5.5-mm. thick, which doesn’t sound like much compared to the iPad’s seven-mm. thickness, but it’s a noticeable difference when you’re holding it.

The S11 has storage options of 128GB, 256GB, or 512GB, which you can add to via the microSD card slot that accepts cards up to 2TB in size. Samsung puts battery life on the S11 at an impressive 18 hours of constant video playback. That’s a full eight hours longer than any of Apple’s iPads and five hours longer than Amazon’s Fire tablets.

Included with the S11 is Samsung’s S Pen stylus for sketching and note-taking tasks. For those who want a keyboard to hammer out longer emails or reports, Samsung’s Book Cover Keyboard Slim adds just that, along with an extra layer of protection.

The Tab S11’s biggest downside is price. You’ll pay a premium over Apple’s standard iPad and even the iPad Air. But that’s the price you pay for the best Android tablet experience currently available.

Operating system: Android with Alexa Tablet UI | Display: 12-inch (2560 x 1600, 2.5K) | Storage: 64GB, 128GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 15 hours | Cellular: None

Amazon surprised everyone in October 2026 when it announced an entirely new collection of Alexa tablets, discontinuing its long-standing and super-affordable Fire Tablet lineup. Along with a refreshed design, the entire software experience has been revamped, unlocking access to the Google Play Store and its millions of apps (including Google apps like Chrome and YouTube) alongside Amazon’s own apps and services. It’s an about-face that adds significant value to Amazon’s tablets.

But with that added value comes a price increase, bringing the cost somewhat more in line with other brands’ introductory Android tablet offerings. The Tablet 11 starts at $329 for 64GB of storage and 8GB of memory with $379 doubling the storage to 128GB. That’s up from $140 for the comparable Fire HD 10.

Hardware improvements include a sleek aluminum housing, an 11-inch 2.5K display that’s crisp and sharp, a fingerprint sensor, up to 15 hours of battery life, and an 8-core 2GHz processor. One downgrade I’d be remiss to not mention is the lack of support for adding storage via a microSD card (because of that fact, I recommend going with the 128GB model).

I can’t express just how much nicer the Tablet 11 is to hold and interact with than the Fire HD 10 — it feels like a high-end, premium tablet when it comes to fit, finish, and performance.

Software improvements go beyond wider app availability, providing the best of Amazon and Google’s ecosystems. The Kindle app, for example, not only looks fantastic on the bigger color display, but Amazon has optimized it to extend battery life and ditch any distractions, like notifications. Additionally, Alexa+ integration gives you access to the familiar digital assistant for asking random questions and controlling your smart home. You can also use it to help you complete tasks or provide more information about what’s on the tablet’s screen.

Even though the price of the Tablet 11 is nearly double that of the discontinued Fire HD 10, at $329, it’s still one heck of a value in today’s price-hike climate. And in true Amazon form, just a month after launch, it’s already on sale for $200 in the base configuration for Black Friday.

Operating system: iPadOS | Display: 11-inch or 13-inch | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB, 1TB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 10 hours | Cellular: Optional 5G

Apple’s iPad Air sits between the base model and the more powerful (and expensive) iPad Pro in Apple’s tablet lineup. It’s available in two different sizes: 11 inches and 13 inches, the latter being a fairly recent addition to the iPad Air lineup.

What makes this tablet our top pick for gaming is its Apple M4 processor. That’s the same chip Apple has used in its MacBook lineup, giving you Mac-like power in a tablet form. Add in the fact that the App Store is full of games like Minecraft, Fortnite, Roblox, and Among Us — on top of the Apple Arcade’s extensive (and entertaining) catalogue of games — and you have a massive library of games to choose from. Most games support using a third-party controller from Xbox or PlayStation, adding to the overall gaming experience.

When you’re not gaming, the addition of the Magic Keyboard and an Apple Pencil turn the iPad Air into a device you can get work done on, especially in combination with iPadOS 26’s multitasking features to use multiple apps at the same time.

I’ve been using the 11-inch model paired with Apple’s Magic Keyboard that includes a trackpad. The smaller iPad Air’s display has the same resolution as the standard iPad but features an anti-reflective coating to cut down on reflections and is capable of displaying more vibrant colors.

It’s available in four somewhat subdued colors: blue, purple, Starlight, and Space Gray. Storage options cover the standard 128GB, 256GB, 512GB, and 1TB. Battery life for the iPad Air is ten hours, which is enough for an all-night gaming session.

Between the M4 processor and the performance boost it brings, the mid-range price point, and the App Store’s breadth of games available — the iPad Air is an easy choice for anyone looking for the best gaming tablet.

Operating system: iPadOS | Display: 11-inch or 13-inch OLED | Storage: 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | External storage: USB-C| Battery life: 10 hours | Cellular: Optional 5G

Apple’s iPad Pro tablet lives up to its name by offering the best laptop-replacement experience you can get on an Apple tablet, bar none. Powering the iPad Pro is Apple’s current-generation M5 processor, also found in the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air lineup.

A 13-inch iPad Pro has long been my travel computer, having taken the previous-generation M4 model around the world with me, and I’d have no qualms with swapping it out for the M5 upgrade thanks to the boost in performance. I use it connected to a Magic Keyboard 95 percent of the time and spend the rest of the time using it in my lap along with an Apple Pencil Pro to edit photos. That versatility is something you can’t even get from a Mac (no Apple computer offers a touchscreen), which is why the iPad Pro is the best tablet for professionals.

I’ve been using the 512GB 13-inch model, but Apple offers storage allotments up to 2TB — with 1TB and 2TB models getting a bump up from 12GB of memory to 16GB.

The OLED display’s resolution of 2,752 by 2,064, along with an adaptive refresh rate that goes from 10Hz to 120Hz and a maximum of 1,600 nits brightness, begs to be used for editing photos or videos. You can get the Pro with standard glass or pay a few hundred dollars more for nano-texture glass, which cuts down on reflectivity and, to some, looks better overall.

The downside? You’re going to pay a premium for the laptoplike experience: a laptoplike price as much or more than what what you’d pay for a MacBook Air — especially if you opt for a fully loaded 13-inch iPad Pro, which will set you back more than $2,000.

Operating system: iPadOS 27 | Display: 8.5 inches (2316 x 1512) | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: Ten hours | Cellular: 5G

Apple finally released an iPad Mini with an OLED display. That’s the same type of display Apple has used in the iPhone and some iPad models for years. The benefit of an OLED screen is brighter, more vivid colors with deeper, darker blacks. In short, everything just looks better, and that’s very much the case on the newest iPad Mini.

I prefer to get the bad news out of the way first, so here goes: The iPad Mini now starts at $699, and discounts aren’t common. Ouch. That’s the price for the 128GB model with the cost going up to $799 to double the storage to 256GB, then again to $999 for 512GB. The 256GB and 512GB models can come equipped with an optional Nano-texture glass, similar to what’s used on the internal display of the iPhone Duo, adding $100 to the cost. Oh, and if you want a 5G cellular connection, the price jumps up another $250. All told, you can spend as much as $1,249 on a fully tricked-out iPad Mini.

The good news is the new Mini is loaded with new features, hardware and software alike. The previously mentioned OLED display is larger than the last generation’s. The front-facing camera has been moved from the top to the edge of the landscape screen, perfect for daily video-call use. And the battery now lasts ten hours, matching the rest of the iPad lineup.

Powering the iPad Mini is Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which is capable of all the fancy Siri AI features Apple loves to tout. You can connect the iPad Mini to an external monitor and use it as you would a laptop with multiple apps and windows open across both screens.

In one of the craziest hardware designs I’ve used in recent memory, the Mini lacks any traditional speaker grilles or cutouts. Instead, Apple’s using what it calls an Acoustic Display screen as one big speaker. I was weirded out the first time I started playing music and could feel the screen vibrate under my fingers as I tapped and swiped on the display. I assumed the sound quality would suffer from the new design, but in some ways, I find it to be better — namely because you can’t muffle the speaker while holding the tablet and the sound is being pushed directly at you.

Yes, this year’s iPad Mini is expensive. There’s no getting around that. But it’s also the most capable tablet of this size. It’s small enough to go into an overnight bag, a purse, or even a coat pocket but powerful enough to run multiple apps across multiple screens at the same time.

Operating system: Android with Alexa Tablet UI | Display: 8.7 inches (1340 x 800) | Storage: 64GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 14 hours | Cellular: None

Amazon’s Fire Tablet for Kids lineup has been a staple recommendation for as long as I can remember writing buying guides. They were cheap; offered mediocre performance, access to a deep kid-friendly content library, and comprehensive parental controls; included a case, and had a two-year worry-free guarantee that replaced a broken tablet with no questions asked.

With the $239 Kids Tablet 8, the cost has gone up and Amazon no longer offers its two-year worry-free guarantee — but you still get a case; parental controls; and access to Amazon’s kid-friendly library of apps, games, and videos; along with the added benefit of access to all of the kid-friendly apps and content built into the Google Play Store (including Google’s own parental controls).

The Kids Tablet 8 comes in two versions — one designed for kids ages 3 to 5 and another designed for 6-to-12-year-olds. They’re the same price with the biggest difference between the models being the type of case included. Younger kids get a soft case with options like Paw Patrol or a cool-green colorway, while the older kids get a hard case in an aquatic color or featuring characters such as SpongeBob. Amazon has also tailored the videos, apps, games, and books in its Kids+ offering (a year of which is included in the cost of the tablet) for the specific ages on the respective tablets.

The Amazon Kids Tablet 8 has an eight-inch display, a slim aluminum body that should be harder to damage than the old plastic Fire tablets, up to 14 hours of battery life, 64GB of storage, and 4GB of memory. It’s barebones to some extent but also fully capable of keeping a young child entertained. And similar to the Alexa Tablet 11, while the Kids Tablet 8 is more expensive than its predecessor, it will surely see frequent discounts, like its current Black Friday price of $150, bringing it back in line with what the Fire tablet of old cost.

Operating system: Kindle firmware | Display: 7-inch (300 ppi) | Storage: 16GB | External storage: None | Battery life: 12 weeks | Cellular: None

Amazon’s Kindle line arguably paved the way for the entire e-reader industry. And the current version of the Kindle Paperwhite is the best table for reading. With the most important features for reading packaged at an attractive price, and with full access to the massive Kindle library at your fingertips, it’s an easy choice for all bookworms.

The Paperwhite has a seven-inch display with a resolution of 300 pixels per inch. That means text will look clear and sharp, instead of you seeing each pixel around the edges of letters. And the adjustable backlight allows you to change brightness and color based on your preferences and environment, so you can read almost anywhere. But my favorite part of using the Paperwhite is how fast and responsive turning pages or browsing the Kindle store feels. I have a very old Kindle, and it’s painfully slow. The Paperwhite feels a lot more like other modern tablets.

It comes with 16GB of storage, which may not seem like a lot by comparison with general-purpose tablets, but it is more than enough to hold thousands of books. Amazon puts the battery life at 12 weeks, based on 30 minutes of reading per day. If you have more time to read each day than that, then I envy you.

Amazon has several Kindle models, from the basic Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite to the Kindle Colorsoft and Kindle Scribe. Each one has its own selling points. The Colorsoft has (as you’d expect from the name) a color display, while the Scribe is bigger and doubles as a note-taking tablet.

entry.title: I Stand Behind the Viral $32 Walmart Jeans
entry.summary: It turns out that Scoop’s Stanton stovepipe jeans are the exact right jeans for a 45-year-old.
entry.content:
The other day I was in the East Village, gazing out the window of the salon while my kids got haircuts, and two young girls walked by in low-rise, bootcut Diesel jeans. Suddenly, my head was spinning. Had I unwittingly slipped into a time loop? It seemed possible. After all, the Strokes had recently released a new album and America was waging war in the Middle East on a flimsy pretext. Was I 23 and living in a dingy apartment on Rivington street above a vegan café co-owned by Moby? I shook my head to dispel these visions and looked down to remind myself that in 2026, my legs are encased in the sturdy denim of Scoop “The Stanton” stovepipe jeans.

Choosing jeans, for a person of my exact age (45 years) and tenure in NYC (25.5 years), is existentially fraught. We can’t look back — we can never look back. Low rise — never again. Not in our name. Boot cut — maybe. Maybe. But neither can we wear the extremely high-rise, wide-legged jeans that were popular a split-second ago. You glance around on the street and realize that those jeans are just wrong now.

For me, at least, the answer is the viral Walmart jeans that I first read about in Jenn Romolini’s newsletter, which is a reliably great source of fashion advice for people who want to look okay while also being medium-old. For the price of three iced lattes, I figured it was okay to take a gamble. Jenn’s description — “stretchy but not too stretchy, with a natural-looking wash and the ideal not-too-baggy or slim straight leg, plus a good ass fit” — was exactly what I needed to hear. I also learned from TikTok that they are supposedly a dupe of the Khaite Danielle jean, which are $620. Those jeans have a size range that tops out at 32, making one to one comparison impossible for me, a 34. Also, if the $620 jeans are better than the $32 jeans, which is entirely possible, I don’t really need to know that information.

When my Stanton jeans first arrived, I put them on and found they were, in a word, perfect. I have slim hips and a big/nonexistent waist and wear a size 12-14 depending on whatever mystery logic different brands use. I sized down to a 12 and had no problem zipping them up, meaning they had just enough give to accommodate my gut. The heavy denim flows nicely out from a slim fit at the thigh to a loose, but not baggy, line around the leg. Their one cool trick is that they are 99 percent cotton and 1 percent spandex, which means that they 99 percent look like non-stretch jeans. I wore them to the office and showed them to every Strategist editor I encountered, and all of those women paused to feel the weight of the denim and at least pretended to be impressed. For one editor, I even did a little twirl. Such is the power of the Stanton. Even better news: All of this remained true after I washed them, which I disgustingly had not done before wearing them the first time.

You will not be mistaken for a 25-year-old in these jeans, but that’s kind of the point. They are a compromise, a pair of pants you put on when you want to make a statement and the statement is “I am wearing jeans with a zipper and a non-elasticized waist.” My one caveat is that I’m 5’7’’ and the 30’’ inseam hits just below the ankle on me, making them look good with sneakers or loafers, but on my shorter, curvier friend Sari they puddled a bit at the floor, necessitating a higher heel (she kept them anyway because they’re $32).

entry.title: Everything I Pack in My Go Bag
entry.summary: A pair of dry socks is a game changer.
entry.content:
Whether you’re dealing with a natural disaster, a public-health emergency, or a human-caused disaster, an emergency kit can help you get to safety and stay safe. And having these items packed and ready can give you peace of mind, even if you don’t need to use them. Kits like these — sometimes called go bags or bug-out bags (most of these items can fit in one backpack, so you can get up and go) — should provide you with the basics to survive a few days. When I wrote about the backpacking gear I use to survive in the woods, I listed items that serve an essential purpose, are lightweight, and don’t take up much space in your pack. The same rules apply to the things in a home emergency kit. (If you’re looking for more items to stock up on — especially if you’re looking to shelter in place rather than get up and go — my colleague Kat Gillespie rounded up a list of emergency-preparedness items as recommended by survivalists and emergency professionals.)

The gear you include in your kit might depend on your situation, such as specific medical needs like prescription medications, or whether you have kids, pets, or other family members. The types of items you pack will also depend on your local geography — both because of the types of natural disasters common in the area and also the kind of terrain you might end up in.

You might be surprised by the kit you can put together with what you have lying around the house: Some of the canned goods in your pantry and extra toiletries from your bathroom are perfect for a go bag. And if you don’t already have them, you can easily buy them online or purchase them at your local drug store or supermarket.

Updated on November 24, 2026
We’ve confirmed prices and updated availability for all of the products we recommend.

Food and water are the basic necessities of an emergency kit. Opt for nutritious, nonperishable foods like canned beans and vegetables, protein bars, and energy bars. I like having some extra freeze-dried backpacking meals handy because they’re lightweight and don’t take up much space. It’s also a good idea to bring a water filter in case you don’t have access to clean, drinkable water. Including extra utensils and packable plates or bowls is a good idea, if you have the space. If you have kids and pets, be sure to pack extra food for them too.

A first-aid kit is a crucial part of an emergency kit. Having basic supplies like bandages, gauze, tweezers, adhesive tape, antiseptic wipes, and nonprescription medications will help you be prepared for minor injuries. There are many good kits out there, but I use this one from Adventure Medical Kits. Pack prescription medications (or a list of them), too, along with N95 masks and extra plastic bags and trash bags for sanitary purposes.

It’s always a good idea to have a few travel-size toiletries, like a toothbrush, extra toothpaste, sanitary wipes, soap, shampoo, and other items in your routine to maintain good hygiene and to stay comfortable. If you use them, pack an extra set of contact lenses and backup prescription and reading glasses.

In an emergency, you might not know how long you’ll be away from home. Having a change of dry clothes can not only keep you comfortable but can be crucial in inclement weather. I opt for versatile materials like wool, which insulates and handles moisture well. You’ll also want to pack a rain shell for wet weather.

Take copies (or original versions) of IDs, birth certificates, and insurance in the kit. It’s always a good idea to bring cash. Keep the documents and cash in a sealed container like this one, or a plastic bag.

If there’s a power outage, or if you just need to move around in the dark, you’ll want a light source. Opt for a powerful, compact LED flashlight or headlamp with a long battery life — and if you can, one that’s rechargeable.

Weather radios can be helpful for hearing emergency radio broadcasts and important weather information — they’re tapped into the NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) network, which broadcasts those alerts, whereas regular radios won’t pick up those frequencies. I opt for a model that has a hand crank (which often recharges the battery) in addition to a solar panel.

Keep a few spare batteries and a rechargeable option (like the solar-powered weather radio, which works as a charger) to ensure that your devices will have extra juice when you need it.

A multitool or pocket knife is one of those versatile pieces of equipment that might be crucial for tasks that require pliers, a can opener, scissors, wrenches, screwdrivers, or a knife. I like my Leatherman, which makes all the individual tools easy to pull out and use while being housed in a compact design.

Having maps of your local area (or a GPS device) can help you get your bearings in an emergency. I opt for a device like the Garmin InReach, which provides a digital map of my surroundings and has SOS capabilities.

Keep a little container of matches (in a waterproof case) stashed in your kit. I have the same ones in my backpacking kit and keep them in a plastic bag, along with some kindling — I use extra toilet paper.

A heat-reflective blanket (which often looks like foil) is a lightweight emergency option if you don’t have enough insulation in colder weather. You want to keep a stable core body temperature when you’re exposed to the elements, and this pocket-size layer can help you achieve that in a pinch. And if you need to quickly make a shelter, a waterproof tarp can provide a shield from rain and wind and serve as a makeshift tent. A roll of duct tape will be useful in many situations, including patching fabrics or repairing gear and equipment.

entry.title: The Best Tablets for Kids
entry.summary: We tested Apple, Android, and Amazon tablets for kids to find the best models for children of all ages.
entry.content:
Shopping for a tablet for your kid can be confusing and downright stressful if you don’t know what you’re looking for. Who’s got the best content for children and the best parental controls? Do you go with Apple’s iPad just because it’s an iPad and that’s what you’re using? Or are Amazon’s revamped Kids Tablets more than enough to do the job? What if you’re an Android user and want nothing to do with Apple? Or vice versa?

For over 15 years now, I’ve used and tested dozens of tablets — spanning all of the major operating systems, content ecosystems, and parental-control setups — while raising my own three kids. And let’s be honest: The experience hasn’t all been good.

And so, for the last month, I drew on those years of real-life experience to put a select group of tablets through their paces to find the absolute best options for kids.

Updated on November 24, 2026
We’ve added Amazon’s new Kids Tablets in place of its discontinued Fire tablet predecessors, along with the latest Kindle Kids, and we have checked pricing and confirmed availability for our other recommendations.

The operating system on a tablet naturally dictates the overall experience for you and your child. Among mainstream tablets (meaning not dedicated toy tablets for kids), you have the choice between Apple’s iPadOS and Google’s Android (Amazon has discontinued tablets based on its own Fire OS and its latest models run Android with some Amazon-specific customizations). Both platforms have their own respective parental-control systems baked into the OS, making it easier for you to manage which apps can be installed and set time limits. (I’ll get more into parental controls in a minute.)

Apple’s iPadOS doesn’t offer a dedicated mode for kids. Google includes a Kids Space on its own Pixel Tablet (as well as other models), while Samsung’s tablets feature customized tools that transform the interface into a kid-friendly experience. Amazon’s Kids Tablets include the Kids+ service, that provides access to curated content based on your kid’s age.

The type of phone you own will also be a factor in narrowing down your options based on the operating system, though this is more of an issue for those looking to get an iPad for their kids. Apple’s Screen Time tools can only be managed from an Apple device, whereas Android users can use an app running on either Android or iOS or a dedicated website to adjust settings.

Each operating system has its own parental-control tools. Apple’s Screen Time gives parents near-total control over a child’s device. Time limits, app restrictions, and a bedtime mode that disables the device between set hours — along with more features — are all managed from the parent’s Apple device.

Amazon’s Kids+ service requires a subscription after the initial one-year trial that comes with every Kids Tablet or Kindle. With Kids+, your child gets a dedicated profile on the Amazon device, complete with curated access to content like books, games, apps, and videos based on their age. You can also set time limits and add or remove access to apps directly from the Parent Dashboard app.

Android’s Family Link service is Google’s parental-control offering for Android devices. Using the mobile app or website, you can pull all of the standard parental-control levers for app restrictions, app time limits, and schedules. Furthermore, Samsung Kids brings its own list of controls, many of which mirror Family Link, along with the added bonus of locking the interface in a kid-friendly design.

Google’s Play Store has a dedicated page that lists all teacher-approved apps and games.

Apple’s App Store also has a dedicated section for kids, with arguably the biggest app catalogue for children of all ages. Apple Arcade, a subscription service, gives you and your child unlimited access to hundreds of games with no ads or in-app purchases.

Amazon’s Kids+ and Kindle services include curated apps, videos, games, and books based on the age you select for your child during setup as part of their Kids+ subscription. Amazon tablets also have access to the Google Play Store.

The screen size of a tablet really comes down to the size and weight you think your child can comfortably carry and use. The bigger the display, the bulkier the tablet will be. The screen sizes on our top picks range in size from six inches for a Kindle to 13 inches for the larger models of the iPad Air.

Display quality likely isn’t a factor when shopping for a kid’s tablet — they aren’t counting pixels or old enough to even care if a display panel is AMOLED, as long as the latest episode of Bluey can stream uninterrupted.

Storage is a major factor when it comes to traveling with kids — having enough space to download content ahead of time means you’ll make it through those flights and road trips without protest, and you won’t have to hunt down Wi-Fi as soon as you reach your destination.

Except for the Amazon tablets on our list, all the tablets we selected come with a minimum of 128 GB of storage. The Amazon Kids Tablets start at 64 GB. Kindles with 16 GB of storage have more than enough space for thousands of books.

While some Android tablets have a microSD card slot for memory expansion, neither Amazon’s Kids Tablets nor Apple’s iPad lineup have one. You can, however, plug an external drive into the USB-C port to play downloaded videos that you own. But keep in mind that you can’t save games or download movies from streaming apps to an external drive.

To avoid constantly managing content and running into frequent “storage is full” messages, opting for the most storage you can — a 256 GB model, if you can get it — is a wise choice. Future you will definitely thank present you down the road.

Battery life for nearly all tablets ranges from 10 to 18 hours, which is typically measured by either watching videos or browsing the web continuously. Longer battery life is something we can all agree is a good thing, but unless your child practically lives on their tablet or you’re taking some very long trips without the opportunity to charge, the current standard is more than likely good enough for most families.

Operating system: iPadOS | Dedicated kids mode: No | Parental controls: Screen Time | Display: 11-inch, 2360-by-1640 | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB| External storage: No | Battery life: 10 hours | Cellular: 5G

We recently selected the base iPad as the best overall tablet because of its refined experience, reliable performance, large app library, and its reasonable price tag. For those very same reasons, along with deep parental controls, it’s also our pick as the best tablet for kids overall.

The 11th-generation iPad comes in four fun colors: silver, blue, pink, and yellow. The color isn’t a big deal if you’re planning on putting the iPad in a case, and you have plenty of great kid-friendly options, like the Speck Products CASE-E-RUN case or Belkin’s Toy Story 5 Lilypad case.

It’s equipped with an 11-inch display and weighs just over a pound before adding a case. In comparison, the Fire HD 10 Kids Pro weighs right at a pound and 1.45 pounds with the included case. Battery life is the lowest of the bunch, at ten hours of constant video playback. Storage options are 128 GB, 256 GB, and 512 GB.

The 128 GB model is likely plenty for a young child, but for older children, especially if you have an Apple Arcade subscription with access to hundreds of games, it’s going to fill up quickly.

If your primary device has an Apple logo on it, it’s a breeze to remotely manage all parental controls via Screen Time in the Settings app. If you’re not an Apple user, you can still use Screen Time to control your child’s usage habits, but you’ll need to do it directly on the tablet — just be sure to set a PIN code they can’t easily guess.

Unlike the Tab A11+ and Fire tablets, the iPad lacks any sort of dedicated child mode or even user profiles, which is one of my biggest gripes about getting an iPad for your child. It’s a frustrating omission, especially since a family tablet shouldn’t have to be locked to a single user profile when kids are young.

The best part about getting the iPad for a kid? It’ll grow alongside them. Not only is the App Store packed with age-appropriate apps, but you can add accessories like Apple’s Magic Keyboard Folio or nearly any Bluetooth keyboard and mouse for a laptop-like experience. The iPad also supports the Apple Pencil for sketching, interactive coloring-book apps, or practicing handwriting.

Operating system: Android | Dedicated kids mode: Yes | Parental controls: Samsung Kids | Display: 11-inch (1920 x 1200) | Storage: 128GB | External storage: USB-C, microSD up to 2TB | Battery life: 15 hours | Cellular: No

Samsung’s Galaxy Tab A11+ Kids is a more affordable variant of our top pick for best Android tablet, the Galaxy Tab S11.

At the same price as Apple’s iPad, you get the tablet, a protective case with a handle that doubles as a kickstand, and a stylus that attaches to the case via the included tether.

It has an 11-inch display and weighs 1.1 pounds without the case or 1.6 pounds with the included case.

There’s only one storage option of 128 GB, but you can add a microSD card to increase storage up to 2 TB — and you can install apps, games, or download videos directly to it. Its 15-hour battery life leads the pack among all of the tablets we tested, which is sure to come in handy on long road trips or cross-country flights.

My favorite part of the A11+ Kids is that it’s a full-fledged tablet for parents, but with a single tap of the Kids app, it instantly transforms into an interface built specifically for young kids. There are fun animations and playful characters that randomly appear on the home screen, along with a curated set of apps your kid can download with just a tap. If an app isn’t directly available in Kids mode, you can download it using your Google account and make it available in the kid mode — it’s super easy.

You can set limits and see usage time within the Kids app. When the child is done, you simply enter your passcode or use facial recognition to return to the standard Android tablet experience.

When your child outgrows the playfulness of the Kids app, all of the same apps and content are available in the full-fledged Android experience, which you can control via Google’s Family Link.

Operating system: Alexa Tablet UI | Display: 8.7-inch (1340 x 800) | Storage: 64GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 14 hours | Cellular: None

Gone is Amazon’s Fire tablet lineup, replaced with its new Alexa Tablet and Kids Tablet offerings. With the change comes significant improvements, including full access to Google’s ecosystem of apps and services. That means users now get access to the entire Play Store app catalogue, along with Google’s own apps, like YouTube — and your kids will appreciate that as much as you will.

The transition includes more than software. The Kids Tablet 8 has a new design, ditching the cheap-feeling plastic housing for aluminum. With an 8.7-inch display, the tablet weighs 11.6 ounces before adding the included protective case. Amazon still includes that case at no extra cost when you purchase a Kids Tablet, though the specific kind of case you get depends on the age-specific model you buy.

The $239 Kids Tablet 8 for 3- to 5-year-olds comes with a soft foam case, with your option of Paw Patrol, Cool Green, or Mystic Mountain designs on it, and is easier for young children to hold on to while riding in a car or on a long plane ride. There’s also a version for kids 6 to 12 that includes a slim hard case with Aquatic, SpongeBob, Sunshine Barbie, or Rainbow Cat designs.

Also included is a year of Amazon’s Kids+ service that gives you access to curated age-specific content. After the year expires, it auto-renews at $7.99 a month or $69.99 a year for Prime members. You’re able to add multiple kids’ profiles to the tablet, each one with its own content and app library.

Unfortunately, one feature not carried over from the Fire tablets is the two-year worry-free guarantee that meant Amazon would replace a broken tablet, no questions asked. If your kid breaks it, you’ll need to buy it (again), which is a disappointment. Another feature left behind is support for expandable storage via a microSD card slot. The storage amount you purchase is the storage you’re stuck with, as with Apple’s tablets.

Also, at its regular price of $230, the Kids Tablet 8 is more expensive than its predecessor, though it may be worth it considering you’re no longer locked into Amazon’s limited Fire OS experience. Full Google support and a vastly improved design justify the hike, and the Kids+ content is still compelling for younger users. That said, in true Amazon fashion, the Kids Tablet 8 has already been discounted by as much as $80, and odds are we’ll routinely see similar discounts throughout the year, so with a little patience you should have no problem finding one for Fire tabletlike prices.

Operating system: Alexa Tablet UI | Display: 11-inch (2560 x 1600) | Storage: 64GB, 128GB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 15 hours | Cellular: None

Amazon’s new Kids Tablet lineup consists of two models. There’s the previously mentioned Kids Tablet 8 and the slightly bigger Kids Tablet 11.

At $329, the Tablet 11 costs $90 more than its smaller sibling, but you’re getting some notable hardware upgrades in exchange for the added cost. For starters, the display is now 11 inches, and it comes with a fairly big jump in resolution at 2.5K, 2560 x 1600 versus the Tablet 8’s 1340 x 800 screen. That equates to better-looking graphics in games, apps, and videos. The Kids Tablet 11 stays with 64 GB of storage and no microSD card slot, but doubles the memory to 8 GB. That added memory should provide a better overall experience, especially for older kids who are more likely to use resource-intensive games or use multiple apps at the same time. And with 15 hours of battery life, it’s got plenty of juice to keep your kids entertained — especially when traveling.

Software-wise, you’ll get access to Amazon’s Kids+ library of age-appropriate content, which includes games, apps, videos, and books. But with the addition of support for Google apps and services, you’ll also have access to the Google Play Store and, for the first time on an Amazon-branded tablet, YouTube. You can use Amazon’s parental-control dashboard side-by-side with Google’s Family Link parental controls to limit screen time, approve app installs, and the like.

As with the Kids Tablet 8, Amazon includes a case with the Kids Tablet 11. Its design depends on the age range you select when purchasing the tablet. For kids ages 3 to 5 you get a bulky, foam case that’s easier for little kids to hold. For kids 6 to 12, you get a slim, hard-shell case that doesn’t look as dorky. You can select age-appropriate designs for the cases, or opt for a single color.

Again, the main downside of the Kids Table 11 is the big price jump over the earlier Fire version, but again, regular promotions and sales should mitigate that. For example, Amazon currently has it marked down 33 percent ahead of Black Friday. As is usually the case with Amazon, discounts like that pop up frequently.

Operating system: iPadOS | Dedicated kids mode: No | Parental controls: Screen Time | Display: 11-inch or 13-inch | Storage: 128GB, 256GB, 512GB, 1TB | External storage: USB-C | Battery life: 10 hours | Cellular: Optional 5G

Apple’s iPad Air makes a big jump in price along with a big jump in performance. That’s not to say the base iPad’s performance is bad, but the iPad Air’s M4 processor is the same chip used in some of Apple’s Mac lineup. In a tablet, it’s impressively smooth and fast.

Storage options start at 128 GB and top out at 1 TB. You can connect an external drive to the USB-C port for easy access to files without taking up extra space on the device itself. Battery life sticks to the same ten hours as the standard iPad.

The iPad Air is available in two sizes — 11- or 13-inch — and comes in space gray, blue, purple, and starlight. It weighs nearly the same as the base iPad, but odds are if you’re getting this for an older kid to use for schoolwork, you’ll be adding a keyboard accessory such as Apple’s Magic Keyboard, which increases the overall weight to be on par with a MacBook.

You can even connect the iPad Air to an external display through the USB-C port, using both screens like you would a laptop in a similar setup — complete with resizable windows you can move between screens. In fact, those resizable windows work even when using the iPad Air sans an extra display, allowing you to multitask even if things get a little cramped on an 11-inch display.

Parental controls through Apple’s Screen Time are available, and the large app selection from the App Store is sure to make it easy for you and your kid to find the apps they want and are allowed to use.

Operating system: Kindle firmware | Dedicated kids mode: Yes | Parental controls: Kids+ | Display: 7-inch (300 ppi) | Storage: 16GB | External storage: None | Battery life: 12 weeks | Cellular: No

For parents who want a device that will foster a love for reading and encourage a child’s imagination, Amazon’s Kindle Kids Paperwhite is a great choice. Unlike Amazon’s tablets, which have a healthy selection of apps, games, videos, and books, the Kindle is limited to just books. It comes with a free case — you can choose from two kid-friendly designs — plus a year of Amazon’s Kids+ subscription, which will give them access to thousands of books written for kids ages 6 to 12. That’s plenty of content to keep them reading for years to come, and if they run out of books that appeal to them, the Kindle supports books checked out from the library through Libby as well.

With a seven-inch display, 16 GB of storage, and a battery life that lasts up to 12 weeks, it has storage for thousands of books, and you’ll rarely have to worry about plugging it in. It’s also waterproof (it’s rated IPX8, so it can withstand immersion for up to an hour), so it works in the bath or at the beach, and can weather those unavoidable spills and occasional dunkings. The Parent Dashboard app lets you set time limits, give access to more books, and view your kid’s Kindle usage and reading habits.

There’s also a new standard Kindle Kids that runs $50 cheaper, but it isn’t waterproof, has a smaller screen, and only offers half the battery life, so we think stepping up to the Paperwhite is a better bet. Have a kid with a taste for comics and need color? Amazon also offers a Kindle Colorsoft Kids that features a seven-inch color display, though it costs about $70 more.
