entry.title: The Best TVs Under $1,000, According to Experts
entry.summary: A great TV doesn’t need to cost as much as a car. We asked the experts what to look for to get the best looking and sounding TV for your money.
entry.content:
Buying one of the best TVs used to mean spending a lot more than $1,000, but that situation has changed over the last few years. One reason is that relative newcomers such as Hisense and TCL have successfully challenged the supremacy of stalwarts like Samsung, Sony, and LG by offering high-quality TVs at reasonable prices. Another is that brands such as Roku and Amazon — known for making popular streaming devices — have themselves entered the TV market, selling affordable models that feature some of the cutting-edge technologies formerly found only in more premium TVs.

So if you’re looking for a great TV and want to spend under $1,000, you will now find a wide range of options to choose from — so many that you may find yourself needing a little help in narrowing the field. To that end, I enlisted a quartet of TV experts to suggest tips on what features and specifications to look for when shopping and to suggest the under-$1,000 TVs they’d personally recommend. As someone who has been writing about TVs for more than two decades, I feel qualified to add my own suggested TVs — some of which I’ve personally tested — to that list.

Updated on November 24, 2026
We’ve replaced out-of-stock TVs with the latest models: the TCL QM7K has been replaced with the QM6K while the LG B5 has been replaced by the LG B6E. We have also confirmed availability and pricing for the rest of our TV recommendations.

With a budget under $1,000, you won’t find models that deliver the very highest levels of performance when it comes to color, contrast, and brightness. And to get the most for you money, with a few exceptions you’ll likely be looking at the 55-inch screen size. But if you keep an eye out for specific features, you can get a great TV for the money. These features make the difference between a cheap, basic TV and a higher-performing — yet still budget-priced — model.

Almost all TVs above a few hundred dollars support 4K resolution, which provides four times as many pixels as standard HD resolution TVs for a more detailed-looking picture. Aside from 4K, one feature to pay attention to is high dynamic range (HDR) support. “HDR helps you see details in shadows and dark areas of the screen,” says James Holland, a TV reviewer for TechRadar. “Ideally, a TV will have Dolby Vision, HDR10+, and HLG format support.”

It’s important to note that not all TVs support all HDR formats — Samsung favors HDR10+ over Dolby Vision for its TVs, while LG models feature Dolby Vision but not HDR10+. Most other TV brands support Dolby Vision, HDR10+, and HLG, however, and that carries over to under-$1,000 models.

Anyone shopping for an under-$1,000 TV should primarily be looking at LED and mini-LED models, rather than the latest OLED models. Those terms refer to the types of tech used in an LCD TV’s backlight (LEDs are used to illuminate the LCD panel), and the specific backlighting tech version found on different TVs can have a big effect on picture quality.

“If the TV you have in mind says ‘edge lit’ or ‘edge-based lighting,’ steer clear,” says Nick Pino, managing editor, TV & AV at Tom’s Guide. “This means that all the lighting elements are located on the perimeter of the screen rather than behind the LCD panel, and that results in a dimmer picture with worse contrast than TVs with ‘full array’ lighting.”

Beyond full-array lighting, a TV’s local dimming capability also impacts picture quality. Asked to define this feature, TechRadar’s James Holland replied, “It means the backlighting on a TV consists of multiple individual zones that light up different portions of the screen, which helps to improve picture contrast and clarity. The more local dimming zones the better, and while TVs under a grand probably won’t specify how many zones there are — after all, they can’t compete with more expensive, better TVs in this area — the manufacturer should at last advertise that the TV has ‘full local array dimming’ or language to that effect.”

TV shoppers on a strict budget may mostly be limited to LED and mini-LED models, but there are a few under-$1,000 OLED TV options in the smaller screen size (55 inches and under) range. “OLED is widely regarded as superior to mini-LED because each individual pixel can be turned on and off,” says Tom’s Guide’s Nick Pino. “This results in deeper black levels and incredible contrast.”

Chris Boylan, TV and AV editor at eCoustics, is similarly bullish on OLED tech, even at the budget range. “Shoppers who value picture performance over everything else may be able to find an entry-level OLED TV from LG, Samsung or Panasonic for under $1,000, though you might need to look at the previous year’s models in order to find the best deals.”

While a fan, Boylan also cautions that OLED TVs might not be a good fit for all viewing environments: “At the entry-level $1,000 price point, OLED TVs can be a little less bright than comparably priced LED and mini-LED models, which means they may not be the best choice for bright rooms.”

There are other shopping considerations for viewers who typically watch TV shows in bright room lighting. “If you watch mainly during the day in a bright room, how the TV’s screen handles glare will be really important,” says Residential Systems’ John Sciacca. Budget TVs tend to lack the anti-reflective screen coatings found in higher-end sets, so it will be important to check both manufacturer specifications and reviews of particular models to see if they provide an anti-glare feature. High picture brightness also helps reduce the effects of screen glare, and while budget TVs tend to have lower brightness than pricier ones, models that use mini-LED backlighting are generally brighter than both standard LED and OLED TVs.

A high refresh rate is another feature increasingly found in TVs priced under $1,000, and it’s one that TechRadar’s James Holland finds to be important. “While the basic 60Hz is more than enough for movies and typical TV shows, getting a TV with a higher refresh rate of at least 120Hz will help with a clearer, smoother image for sports and gaming.”

For sports, a 120Hz or higher refresh rate can reduce the level of motion blur in fast-action games, and it also helps to eliminate judder (a picture artifact where objects take on a “wobbly” look in shots with camera motion) in movies. The latest generation Xbox and PlayStation consoles also support games with a 120Hz output, which requires a TV with a 120Hz refresh rate to take advantage of that feature.

With relative newcomers such as Hisense, TCL, Amazon, and Roku broadening the TV field, brand is a less crucial consideration than it used to be. Still, there are reasons to stick with a particular brand. “If buying multiple TVs for a home, I’d recommend getting all the same brand,” says Residential Systems’ John Sciacca. “This will provide a similar user experience from room to room without having to learn how to navigate different interfaces.”

By “interfaces,” Sciacca means both a set’s menu and remote-control layout and its smart-TV interface, a subject that Chris Boylan of eCoustics has plenty to say about. “In the $500 to $1,000 range, there aren’t huge differences in TV performance. Most budget TVs from major brands like Samsung, TCL, Hisense, Sony, and LG offer solid picture performance, so I’d recommend looking closely at the user interface, because this will impact your enjoyment of the TV over time.”

As for interface differences between brands, here’s what Chris Boylan had to say: “Amazon’s Fire TV platform is robust but can be a bit ad-heavy. Google TV, as found on Sony, TCL, and Hisense, also offers a wide selection of apps and gaming options but favors YouTube in its search results. LG’s WebOS is a spiffy operating system, but some find their magic remote a bit unwieldy. Samsung also offers a proprietary OS called Tizen, which offers a good selection of apps without much in the way of advertising. And both LG and Samsung offer five- to seven-year OS updates so you know your TV won’t be outdated in its user interface or streaming-app access in just a few years.”

John Sciacca, an AV-product reviewer for Residential Systems who has also designed and installed custom systems professionally for over 28 years, recommends wall-mounting any TV you buy: “This not only gets it to a good viewing height, but it also makes the room feel deeper because you are eliminating that eye-stopping point of the TV sitting two feet in front of the wall.”

To that, I’d recommend that you buy a soundbar along with your TV. TVs in the budget range tend to have lower-powered, downward-firing built-in speakers, and the sound from these can lack clarity, especially with movies. Even a low-cost soundbar can provide a significant audio-quality improvement, improving both dynamics and dialogue intelligibility.

Screen size: 55 to 98 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support; Audio: 2-channel Dolby Atmos and DTS:X audio with Dolby Atmos FlexConnect support; Smart platform: Google TV

Each one of our experts mentioned TCL’s QM7 series TVs as a top under-$1,000 pick. John Sciacca cited the new 55-inch QM7L’s high picture brightness as one factor that would make it a great option for viewing in a well-lit room, and that same quality would enhance any movies watched in HDR. The QM7L is also the least expensive TCL TV to feature the company’s new Super Quantum Dot technology, which expands the set’s color range beyond what most TVs are typically capable of displaying. An anti-reflective screen helps to reduce screen glare on the QM7L, which uses the Google TV smart platform for streaming and features Audio by Bang & Olufsen built-in sound.

Screen size: 55 to 98 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 4 x HDMI (including 2 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support); Audio: 2.1-channel Dolby Atmos and DTS:X audio; Onkyo speaker system; Smart platform: Google TV

TCL carried over its 2025 regular Quantum Dot (QD) mini-LED TVs for 2026, and those models are now seeing strong discounts over their initial release prices. Of these, the entry-level QM6K series offers the most impressive bang for the buck. Along with enhanced color, the QM6K’s Quantum Dot display panel delivers pictures with high brightness, and TCL’s Halo Control technology ensures that contrast is solid and that shadows look uniformly black. With 144Hz support, the QM6K is also a great budget-gaming-TV option and it has powerful sound courtesy of its Onkyo-designed 2.1-channel, 40-watt speaker array.

Screen size: 55 to 116 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 4 x HDMI ports (including 2 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support); Audio: 2.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos and DTS:X audio; Smart platform: Google TV with Gemini Assistant

The Hisense U7 series tops James Holland’s list of under-$1,000 TVs, and the new Hisense U7SG can be found for less than $750 in a 55-inch screen size. This TV’s high brightness and anti-reflection screen make it another great option for bright-room viewing, and with a specified 3,000 local dimming zones, it also has powerful contrast and deep blacks for movies. The U7SG’s native 165Hz display makes it a solid option for both console and PC gaming, and its Google TV smart interface is enhanced with the Gemini Interactive AI feature.

Screen size: 55 to 100 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 3 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 165Hz support; Audio: 4.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos and DTS:X audio; Smart platform: Google TV

The Hisense U8QG series was one of the best TVs I personally tested in 2025, and it’s a steal at its current discounted price. This TV also delivers exceptional brightness, and that factor, plus its anti-reflection screen, makes it perfect for viewing in bright rooms. Like the new Hisense U7SG series, the U8QG also has powerful local dimming for movies and 165Hz support for gaming. Google TV is also onboard for streaming, but the U8QG lacks the Gemini Interactive AI feature found on 2026 Hisense TVs.

Screen size: 55 to 77 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10; Inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 120Hz support; Audio: Two-channel Dolby Atmos; Smart platform: webOS

The LG B6E’s predecessor, the LG B5, was a unanimous top pick among our experts owing to its use of OLED technology, which is known for rich color reproduction and superior contrast compared to mini-LED TVs. The new B6E carries over everything that made the B5 good, and it even bests it in terms of picture brightness, a traditional shortcoming of OLED TVs.

The B6E is also an excellent gaming TV with 120Hz support for Xbox and PlayStation 5 consoles, and its webOS smart-TV platform has been updated with LG Gallery+ for displaying artwork, including ones you generate yourself with the TV’s built-in AI assistant. At the current $700 price for the 55-inch model, the LG B6E is an outstanding value for an OLED TV.

Screen size: 55 to 75 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 120Hz support; Audio: Two-channel Dolby Atmos; Smart platform: Roku OS

James Holland is a fan of the Roku Pro series TV, which, at around $650 in the 55-inch screen size, is an affordable option for a mini-LED TV with a Quantum Dot display panel. At that price, there are some compromises — James cited its lower brightness compared to TCL and Hisense mini-LED TVs, and also its lower dimming-zone count — but the overall picture quality is great for the price. Roku also has a simple, elegant smart TV interface that makes other smart platforms look cluttered in comparison. Yet another benefit to the Roku Pro series is its shadowbox design. According to James, this “lets it sit flat on the wall like a painting when mounted and also allows Roku to engineer more robust audio solutions (and therefore better sound) than you find in most affordable TVs.”

Screen size: 55 to 98 inches; Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+; Inputs: 4 x HDMI ports (including 2x HDMI 2.1 ports with 120Hz support); Audio: Two-channel Dolby Atmos and DTX:X audio; Smart platform: Google TV

An avowed Sony fan, John Sciacca finds the Sony Bravia 5, a 2025 model, to be a solid under-$1,000 TV choice. “Sony has (arguably) the best video processing in the industry, which will result in smoother motion handling, and a sharper, more detailed picture.” John further appreciates the Bravia 5’s “bright and colorful image” and “cinematic black levels” and finds its Google smart-TV platform “easy to navigate,” with “support for virtually any streaming app you can think of.” The Bravia 5 is also “perfect for PlayStation 5,” with processing that automatically optimizes the picture for gaming when a PS5 console is connected. Sony TVs tend to be pricier than the competition, and the 55-inch Bravia 5 lists for $1,399. It can frequently be found on sale for under 1,000, however, and at that price it’s a solid value.

entry.title: The Best TVs Under $500, According to Experts
entry.summary: Budget TVs are better than ever, so we asked the experts to find the best truly affordable sets for movies, sports, and even gaming.
entry.content:
Let’s get this out of the way: There are plenty of TVs to choose from under $500 these days, including models with screen sizes as large as 75 inches. But shopping for the best TV under $500 can be like negotiating a minefield. Low-cost TVs typically have severe enough picture-quality shortcomings that once you get an eyeful, you may want to pack it back in its box and return it.

To prevent that from happening (it’s hard to get a 75-inch set back in the box), I’ve put together this guide to the best TVs under $500. I’ve also asked a team of experts to weigh in on what matters when it comes to TVs in the under-$500 price range, so you’ll know exactly what features and specifications to look out for when shopping.

Updated on November 24, 2026
We’ve replaced out-of-stock TVs with the latest models, with the Hisense U6 Pro replacing the older U56QF and the Samsung Neo QN70H taking the place of last year’s Q8F, and we’ve confirmed availability and pricing for the rest of our recommendations.

For TV shoppers with a budget of $500 or under, the good news is that key features like 4K resolution and HDR, previously found only in the best TVs under $1,000, have migrated down to the under-$500 price range and are now standard. You’ll even find advanced tech like mini-LED illumination and gaming-friendly high refresh rates in the best budget TVs. As long as you’re content with a 55-inch or smaller screen size, you can find a set with surprisingly good picture quality for cheap.

The TV brand you select is more important than ever when you’re looking at the under-$500 price range. You’ll find plenty of budget offerings from big electronics brands like Toshiba, Pioneer, Insignia, Westinghouse, and Onn, but these generally underperform compared to models from brands you may be less familiar with but are actually more established as TV manufacturers.

TCL and Hisense are two brands that have emerged as value leaders over the past few years by providing high-performance features that enhance picture quality even in their entry-level TVs. Samsung, Sony, and LG also make good budget TVs, though the picture quality isn’t nearly as impressive as the pricier models from those brands.

Two other relatively new TV brands are Roku and Amazon, both of which offer budget models with a strong emphasis on usability — they’re experts in the smart-TV interface for streaming, and they’ve brought that to their TVs. “A lot of people really like the Roku interface, which is easy to use and offers voice control,” says John Sciacca, a custom-installation pro and AV product reviewer for Residential Systems. Voice control is also a reason that James Holland, a TV reviewer for TechRadar, finds Amazon’s budget TVs appealing: “Do you care about hands-free control? Any of Amazon’s TVs except the 2- and 4-Series can do that.”

Finding a TV with 4K resolution for under $500 used to be a tough task, but that feature has now become fairly standard for the price range. Two less standard features that can have a big impact on picture quality are mini-LED backlights and full array local dimming, and an increasing number of under-$500 TVs are starting to provide both.

LCD-based TVs such as the models listed in this guide use either standard LED or mini-LED backlighting to illuminate their LCD panels and create their pictures. The benefit of mini-LED is that the lamp modules in the backlight are significantly smaller than standard LEDs, so there are more modules packed in the array to light up the screen, resulting in brighter, more uniform pictures. Full array local dimming, which can be found on both standard LED and mini-LED TVs, is a process that allows different areas of the screen to be lit up at varying brightness levels. The benefit to this is stronger picture contrast, along with uniform blacks free of the “screen clouding” effects that typically plague cheap TVs that lack local dimming.

Nick Pino, managing editor for TV & AV at Tom’s Guide, strongly recommends budget shoppers look for a mini-LED TV with full array local dimming at minimum. “Not only are these TVs evenly backlit, but they come with a large number of contrast control zones that prevent blooming, or bright elements that bleed into the dark parts of the screen.”

Another high-performance feature that has recently started to show up on TVs in the under-$500 price range is quantum dots, a layer of semiconductor particles that work to improve the efficiency of the TV’s display panel, bringing enhanced brightness and color saturation. LED and mini-LED TVs lacking a quantum-dot layer generally have duller-looking pictures with less vivid colors than models providing that feature, so it’s one well worth paying a bit extra for in an under-$500 TV.

Along with 4K, another feature that’s become pretty much standard for most under-$500 TVs is high dynamic range (HDR) capability, which lets TVs display programming encoded in a format that allows for expanded brightness levels to bring out increased detail in picture highlights and shadows. Movies and TV shows — and even some sports — encoded with HDR are common on streaming services such as Netflix, Disney+, and HBO Max, and a TV with HDR support can display these programs.

There are multiple flavors of HDR, with HDR10 being a base format that’s supported by all streaming services and HDR-capable TVs. Beyond HDR10, there is Dolby Vision, HDR10+, and HLG (hybrid log-gamma), which is a format used mainly for live TV broadcasting. Dolby Vision and HDR10+ are similar in that both are dynamic formats where the picture’s brightness range is optimized on a scene-by-scene basis. Many budget TVs, including models from TCL, Hisense, Roku, and Amazon, support the full range of HDR formats. TVs from Samsung, Sony, and LG, on the other hand, provide more limited HDR support, with Samsung omitting Dolby Vision, and Sony and LG omitting HDR10+.

Yet another feature previously limited to high-priced TVs that’s since migrated down to the budget range is high refresh-rate support. A typical low-cost TV used to have a refresh rate (the number of times per second a video image is displayed onscreen) limited to 60Hz, but you can now find models with 120Hz or even higher refresh rates. The importance of this feature is that it allows you to take advantage of the 120Hz output capability of the latest generation of gaming consoles (and even higher rates for PC gaming). A high refresh rate results in smoother, more realistic motion overall, not just when gaming, so it can also benefit sports on TV by helping to reduce the blur effect in fast-action plays. A high refresh rate on a TV can also improve the look of movies by limiting any judder effects in shots with camera motion.

Chris Boylan, a TV and AV editor at eCoustics, finds a TV’s smart interface to be a major factor to consider when shopping, because it “will dictate your enjoyment of the TV over time.” Boylan prefers the smart interface of LG and Samsung TVs, both of which limit the number of ads you are exposed to, and they also receive regular updates with new features and apps. He also generally likes the Google TV platform found on Sony, TCL, and Hisense TVs but finds the platform to be too weighted toward YouTube in its content search results.

Amazon and Roku both made an initial foray into the TV world through streaming sticks, then eventually launched their own lines of budget TVs that emphasize streaming and smart-home features. Amazon is a good option for those who subscribe to Prime Video or other Amazon services. Amazon TVs can also be used to control the company’s smart devices such as lights, thermostats, and Ring security cameras using Alexa voice commands. Amazon’s smart interface, however, tends to be a bit cluttered and ad-heavy compared to the Roku TV interface, which has a simpler, more streamlined layout.

Screen size: 55 to 98 inches | Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+ | Inputs: 4 x HDMI (including 2 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support) | Audio: 2.1-channel Dolby Atmos and DTS:X audio; Onkyo-designed speaker system | Smart platform: Google TV

Chris Boylan of eCoustic’s top under-$500 TV pick is the 55-inch TCL QM6K: “TCL TVs have extremely competitive pricing and offer solid performance for the money. Personally, I’d spend a bit more for an entry-level OLED or mid-tier mini-LED TV, but if price is the main factor, the QM6K is a solid choice.” This budget mini-LED model features local dimming and TCL’s proprietary Halo Control system to reduce backlight “blooming” artifacts.

As the entry-level mini-LED TV in TCL’s lineup, the QM6K has lower brightness than the company’s step-up models, but it competes favorably there with other TVs in its price range. With support for refresh rates up to 144Hz, the QM6K is a good option for gaming too. It also has a slim, appealing design, and its Onkyo-designed 2.1-channel built-in speakers deliver better-than-average sound for a budget TV.

Screen size: 55 to 100 inches | Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+| Inputs: 4 x HDMI (including 2 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support) | Audio: 2.1-channel Dolby Atmos audio | Smart platform: Amazon Fire TV

TV expert Nick Pino of Tom’s Guide was a fan of the Hisense U65QF series as a budget TV option, and its successor, the Hisense U6 Pro series, steps things up with features like a glare-free screen and AI-based 4K upscaling and motion processing, all while remaining under the $500 price point for the 55-inch model.

Similar to the U65QF, the new series features a QLED display with local dimming, both features typically found in pricier TVs. It’s also a strong gaming TV option, with 144Hz-refresh-rate support and a built-in subwoofer to add drama to video-game soundtracks. High dynamic range support is comprehensive, with Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive, and HLG formats all accounted for, and the U6 Pro runs Amazon Fire TV as its smart-TV platform. While Fire TV might be the key indicator of its budget status — higher-end Hisense TVs use Google TV for streaming — that plaform is a solid option for Prime Video viewers, and the U6 Pro additionally supports Alexa+ voice control.

Screen size: 43 to 85 inches | Formats: HDR10+ | Inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 ports with 144Hz support | Audio: 2-channel Dolby Atmos audio | Smart platform: Samsung Tizen

Samsung isn’t typically thought of as a budget-TV brand, but you can now find the 43-inch version of its QN70H series for under $500. TechRadar’s James Holland recommends Samsung TVs for their comprehensive smart-home integration via the company’s SmartThings platform. Samsung TVs are also well respected for their gaming prowess, and the QN70H series offers both 144Hz support for PC gaming and the built-in Samsung Gaming Hub for cloud-based gaming with apps such as Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now.

Beyond its smart-home and gaming features, the QN70H is part of Samsung’s Neo QLED TV lineup. These models feature a full array Mini-LED backlight that delivers high brightness and refined blacks along with a Quantum Dot display panel for enhanced color. Low-cost Samsung TVs typically don’t provide those premium features, making the 43-inch QN70H a best buy in the Samsung TV family.

Screen size: 50 to 75 inches | Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+ | Inputs: 4 x HDMI ports | Audio: 2-channel Dolby Atmos audio | Smart platform: Amazon Fire TV

Amazon recently rebranded its Fire TV lineup as Amazon Ember TVs, and the newest model can be found in a 50-inch screen size for $419. For that price, you’re getting a QLED display panel with standard LED illumination. Brightness and contrast are below what you’ll get from mini-LED TVs with local dimming, and the refresh rate tops out at 60Hz.

But viewers who live in the Amazon universe, through either a Prime subscription or Alexa smart-home devices, will find much to appreciate here, with innovative features such as hands-free voice control and OmniSense, which uses built-in sensors that can automatically wake the TV or display artwork when you enter the room.

When you’re shopping for Amazon TVs, you’ll also come across the less expensive Ember 4-Series, but that lacks the QLED panel and won’t provide as good a picture; if you are willing to spend a bit over $500, you could look at the Ember mini-LED series, but you’ll likely prefer the Hisense U6, which delivers an Amazon Fire experience with those features at a better price.

Screen size: 55 to 75 inches | Formats: Dolby Vision and HDR10+ | Inputs: 4 x HDMI ports | Audio: 2-channel Dolby Atmos audio | Smart platform: Roku OS

Even when it comes to budget TVs, “bigger is always better,” says John Sciacca of Residential Systems, who finds the Roku Plus Series to be a “standout choice” owing to its picture quality and $479 price for a 65-inch screen size. That truly is a bargain for a 65-inch mini-LED TV with local dimming and a QLED display.

The Plus Series lacks 120Hz support for gaming, making it a better choice for those who simply want to stream movies and shows via Roku’s streamlined, clutter-free smart interface. Like other smart TVs, the Plus Series can control smart-home devices using its voice remote, and it can also be paired with the company’s wireless speakers and subwoofers for enhanced audio.

entry.title: The Very Best Portable Firepits
entry.summary: For marshmallow roasting, meat grilling, and everything in between.
entry.content:
One of the best parts of spending time outdoors is ending the day by relaxing around a campfire. If you’re allowed to safely start a fire, using a portable firepit is both a fun and efficient way to enjoy a fire in nature. (Make sure to check for burn bans in your area by visiting your local park’s or state’s website — these rules will most likely be posted at camp if you’re at a campsite.) In addition to heat and ambiance, a firepit can provide entertainment and a cooking surface, as many can be fitted with grill tops.

Firepit technology has become more advanced in the past decade. Nowadays you can find wood- or wood-pellet-fueled pits advertised as “smokeless,” meaning they have airflow features that keep the fire burning cleanly. Gas- or propane-fueled firepits really deliver on that claim, effectively eliminating smoke altogether.

Updated on November 20, 2026:
We’ve added three new propane-fueled firepits, along with updated testing information, and have confirmed the latest pricing and availability for all our recommendations.

Most portable firepits burn wood or wood pellets, and building a fire in them is similar to building one in a fire ring at a campsite: You use tinder, kindling, and fuel such as larger logs (some wood-burning models can also be fueled with wood pellets). Other models use propane or natural gas; these require a hookup to a propane tank or other gas source.

The benefits of gas-powered firepits are that they’re extremely easy to start (you just turn them on as you would a gas-powered grill), they’re very low maintenance and require little cleanup since there are no leftover ashes or embers to deal with, and they are fully smoke free. Gas-powered firepits actually function like gas-powered heaters as the radiant elements around the fire, rather than the flame itself, provide the majority of the heat.

You’ll also find that some tiny, tabletop-size firepits use isopropyl alcohol, i.e., rubbing alcohol you can pick up at the drugstore, to create a small flame.

All these firepits are designed to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios, from the patio to a picnic. I’ve noted their weights and specific features that make them easier to carry and move around, like grab handles, foldable legs, and carrying cases.

Smoke is caused when particles of the fuel source, such as bits of wood, don’t burn all the way and are carried into the air by the flame. A “smokeless” firepit sounds like an oxymoron, but some wood-burning models are designed to provide air to the base of the flame, which makes it burn efficiently and cleanly, resulting in fewer particles being carried by the flame, and therefore less smoke. I’ve noted each wood-burning model’s ability to provide airflow below: low (little or no airflow features); medium (some airflow features); and high (efficient airflow features).

Gas- and propane-powered or isopropyl-alcohol-fueled models will have a “high” smoke-control rating since they won’t naturally create smoke.

Fuel source: Wood or pellets | Portability: 23.3 lbs.; optional cover, optional handle | Smoke control: High

The stainless-steel Bonfire 2.0 with the bundled stand is the firepit that we’d recommend to most people. It burns efficiently, is easy to use, and looks just as good as a backyard centerpiece as it does at camp. It looks like a simple steel can —which it is — but it’s built with a series of holes that provide airflow to the bottom of the flame. The result is an efficient fire with minimal smoke. Adding the stand not only improves air flow but also keeps the bottom out of the dirt and puts the fire at a nicer height. Outdoor-gear writer Jakob Schiller likes his Bonfire 2.0 because it gives him peace of mind when building fires in nature. “It contains the fire, so you’re not as worried about the fire spreading to the ground, and helps it breathe,” he says.

I’ve had one in my backyard for three summers, and it’s developed an attractive patina. I love how easy it is to light: Just a bit of newspaper and cardboard is enough to get logs burning without much kindling. While I like how much less smoke it produces than a typical firepit, the logs do burn quicker than you’d expect. (This isn’t a problem for me in Vermont, but might be disappointing in areas where firewood is more expensive.) After three years of use, the Bonfire 2.0 still feels sturdy and the exterior is unscathed but for a few small dents accumulated from moving or cleaning it. However, the bottom is starting to show signs of corrosion, despite my efforts to cover it when not in use. (I suspect this may be due to the fact that I didn’t buy the stand with my original purchase.) You can buy additional accessories from Solo Stove, like a pellet adapter, or heat deflector, among others. —Michael Zhao

Fuel source: Wood or pellets | Portability: 31 lbs.; grab handle; optional carrying case / Smoke control: High

The Breeo Y-Series is a worthy upgrade for people who mostly plan to use their firepits at home or while tailgating. At 31 pounds, it’s nearly 50 percent heavier than the Solo Stove Bonfire, but the Y-Series is much nicer to use once the fire is lit. It’s a smokeless firepit but has fewer holes than the Bonfire, which means logs last a bit longer before dissolving into ash. I also appreciate its built-in legs, thicker steel construction, and superior heat distribution (no heat deflector required). It also happens to be made in the USA.

I tested the Y-Series in several locations over the span of several weekends earlier in the summer and love how easy it is to use and clean. The built-in handle helps by allowing you to simply tip out the ashes, even if the unit is still slightly warm. The thick stainless-steel sides are exceptionally sturdy-feeling — it’s hard to imagine this ever denting — and also do a better job of retaining and radiating heat than their thinner competitors.

I also appreciate that the extendable legs stow for transportation and can extend to a shorter height for vibes, and a higher one for ergonomic grilling, using the Outpost grill add-on. The add-on is just as sturdy as the Y-Series itself and plugs right into a socket on the side of the pit. From there, it can be raised, lowered, and rotated to adjust temperature — much like the grills you find built into firepits at some campgrounds. Its 19-inch diameter looks small but easily fits six large burger patties with room to spare. I like the novelty of cooking over a wood fire, but if you prefer a more controlled burn, the Y-Series is designed to work with pellets and lump charcoal without requiring an additional adapter plate. —M.Z.

Fuel source: Propane | Portability: 39.9 lbs.; optional cover | Smoke control: High

Until this year, my main experience with Ninja was with its kitchen appliances, which are so well made I’ve been using the same Ninja blender for over a decade. The Fireside360 is Ninja’s first outdoor firepit and is built with the same efficiency and easy-to-use controls as anything I’ve tested from the brand. The Fireside360 arrived blessedly intact: I just had to pull it out of the box and install the included AAA battery into the control housing. From there, it lit instantly and warmed up within seconds.

The design is simple and uncluttered with two knobs that give you fine control of the heat and flame. As with other gas-powered firepits, the flame is there mostly for ambiance; it provides some heat, but most of the output comes from the heat ring, which has perforations to allow airflow and increase radiant energy. The Fireside360 is smaller and more portable than other models, though we maxed out the seating with four people around the fire. Ninja says you can seat six around the unit, but we felt warmer with four people sitting closer.

I haven’t managed to go through an entire propane tank, but Ninja says it can run for 26 hours on a 20-pound tank at its lowest setting and up to six hours at its highest. The circular heat is similar to the Howl (see below) in that it radiates outward rather than losing heat upward, and at just under 40 pounds, it’s lighter and more portable than many other firepits. The cover is sold separately, and I recommend spending the $50 to protect the stove when it’s not in use — though I did leave it uncovered when it dumped snow overnight, and it still lit up easily the next day. —Maggie Slepian

Fuel source: Propane | Portability: 76 lbs.; optional cover | Smoke control: High

The Infinity Flame is Solo Stove’s first propane model, which surprised me considering the brand’s choke hold on the backyard-firepit market. At three and a half feet across, the Infinity Flame has a generous surface area we could easily fit six people around. The tabletop extenders add a nice touch for setting down food or beverages, making the firepit feel like something you’d find on the patio of a fancy hotel.

It’s an absolute joy to relax around and makes for an excellent patio centerpiece and gathering place. A metal cover turns the firepit into a table when not in use, pulling double duty by protecting the burners from the elements and providing a flat surface for food and small items. The tank platform swivels out for easy propane-tank swaps, and the single-knob control panel is easy to use once you figure out how far to turn the knob.

You will want to set aside some quality time to build this one (or rejoice at the opportunity if you are into DIY) because the Infinity Flame arrives extremely not in one piece. I’m pretty handy and it still took me two hours to put together on my own. I also had some trouble getting it to light. The pilot was finicky, and it took a few tries to get the stove to ignite. —M.S.

Fuel source: Wood or pellets | Portability: 8 lbs.; collapsible structure, carrying bag | Smoke control: Medium

If you’re looking for a less bulky firepit, consider this pop-up pit from Fireside Outdoor. It weighs just eight pounds, making it the lightest model on this list (besides the smaller, tabletop-size FLIKR below). I’ve been using the Pop-Up for the past three years and found that its design provides ample airflow to the flame. You rest logs on top of a stainless-steel mesh sheet, which allows air to flow beneath it, up into the base of the fire. Other than the mesh sheet, it doesn’t have any other features that help control smoke; it burns like a normal campfire. I also like how its aluminum walls kept the fire contained — I don’t have to worry about loose ash or bits of charred wood escaping the pit. It collapses into a two-foot-long carrying bag, like a tent. (Because of its slim shape, I keep it stashed in my trunk in case I need to bust it out during a car-camping trip.) —Jeremy Rellosa

Fuel source: Wood or pellets | Portability: 19.8 lbs.; Cover/carrying bag, foldable legs, two carrying handles | Smoke control: High

The BioLite FirePit+ uses the same “smokeless” technology that the Solo Stove Classic does, but takes it up a notch: it has a rechargeable, USB-compatible, battery-powered fan that feeds the flame with air through a network of tubes that surround the burn chamber (like a central air system) to create an ultraclean, smoke-free fire. Strategist contributor James Lynch gave it two thumbs up: “I spent many years as a Boy Scout and a few as a backpacking and canoeing guide, bending over to blow on smoldering twigs, working hard to get the logs to catch, huffing and puffing until I was light-headed. You don’t need to do any of that with the FirePit+,” he writes, noting how the fan helps you start — and keep — the fire going. “Other than finding your grandpa or a nearby Eagle Scout, I don’t think I’ve seen anything that makes building and maintaining a fire easier.”

Because of its ease of use (and the help from the fan), it’s the firepit we recommend for camping: It makes starting fires a breeze (which I find especially welcome after a long day of being outside), it comes with a grate to roast or cook food on top of it, like a hibachi grill, and its two large handles make it easy to carry from your car to wherever you’re setting up. Outdoor writer Ebony Roberts says there’s a slight learning curve to mastering the airflow (which you can control with your phone via a Bluetooth connection to the fan), but she likes its overall design. “The mesh paneling on the sides becomes nearly transparent as the fire burns hot, so you get a nice view of the dancing flames,” she says.

One downside of the BioLite is that it’s almost too efficient at burning fuel. After a few months of testing, I found that I was burning through logs fast — even on the fan’s lowest setting. Schiller agrees: “You burn through a lot of wood, but you never really have to worry about not having a solid fire,” he says. And at 10 inches, its burn chamber is shallow, so you mostly have to burn logs horizontally. —J.R.

Fuel source: Propane | Portability: 20 lbs.; optional carry case | Smoke control: High

I was an early beta tester of the original Howl Campfires firepit back in 2022, and it’s still one of the most portable, innovative designs I’ve ever used. I can carry it with one hand and walk from my truck to the campsite, and it’s sturdy on a range of surfaces. It’s built more for camping, hunting, and fishing outings than for backyard patios — though I’ve used it for all of the above — and its rugged build can stay lit and heated above 10,000 feet and in torrential downpours. And it’s safe to use even during fire bans.

Howl offers three models ranging in price from $374 for the smaller R1 to nearly $1,500 for the R4 MKII. My recommendation is the middle ground: the R3, a good compromise between the portability of the R1 and the output of the R4 MKII. You’ll still pay a premium, but the made-in-the-U.S. design is built for convenience, long-lasting durability, and the best portability-to-heat output I’ve ever tested. Howl claims its BarCoal technology feels like a campfire because the steel tube emits infrared light at the same frequency as wood coals and emits radiant heat outward, rather than just convective heat upward. Whatever the explanation, I’ve tested the Howl on frigid fall evenings at higher elevations in Montana, gathered around it at ice-climbing events, and most recently, used three Howl units as the main source of heat after a winter hiking event where temperatures hovered around 25 degrees. —M.S.

Fuel source: Propane | Portability: 11 lbs.; cover/carrying bag, foldable legs, carrying handle | Smoke control: High

Outdoor-gear reviewer Graham Averill has tested many different firepits including the Solo Stove and BioLite models, but the Ignik FireCan is his current favorite because of its efficiency. It’s gas-powered, so you only have to hook up a propane tank to get your fire started — no need to find kindling or fuss with fire starters. That also means there will be zero smoke since no wood is being burned. “It’s small, puts out enough heat to keep you warm, and is safe to use even if there’s a fire ban,” Averill says. “I use it for tailgating in the fall and winter, like after a day of skiing. It takes aprés ski up a notch, for sure.” Averill also likes how easy it is to load into the back of his truck. It has the look of a retro steel ammunition can but with grates that allow the flame to poke through. The brand also sells rocks that can be added to the can to create a more natural-looking flame, although the rocks are purely aesthetic. —J.R.

entry.title: Hot Wheels, American Girl, LEGO: The Best Advent Calendars for Kids (So Far)
entry.summary: Filled with building toys, science experiments, collectibles, and everything in between.
entry.content:
Even in this economy, the Advent calendar industrial complex is thriving. Sure, it’s still pretty early, but some of this year’s most popular Advent calendars for kids — particularly from NeeDoh and various other squishy brands, LEGO, Clickeez, Wigglitz, Pokémon, Fuggler, and Crazy Aaron’s Thinking Putty — have either started to sell out or are going fast. So it’s definitely worth planning ahead.

If you know a child with their heart set on a NeeDoh Advent calendar this year, your best bet is to stop in at your local independent toy store to inquire about availability and restocks. You can also keep an eye on the NeeDoh calendar at Amazon, just don’t get your hopes up too high, as restocks are haphazard and available to purchase by lottery only — if you get lucky and happen to refresh the product page at the right moment, you may be able to “request an invite” for a chance to buy the calendar at an unspecified future date.

Otherwise, to help you choose from all the other amazing Advent calendars available for kids this year, I’ve pulled together a list of favorites for all ages, filled with building toys, stuffed animals, crafts, collectibles, and everything in between.

Updated on October 29, 2026
I added several new Advent calendars and confirmed the pricing and availabity of all the ones we recommend.

Designed for toddlers, Haba’s Advent calendar is filled with 24 wooden animal figures and comes with a book that tells a daily story about each day’s animal. The box folds out to reveal an illustrated play area for the menagerie.

Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang and her number-obsessed 3.5-year-old son have been making their way through the Numberblocks Advent calendar early, to help with preschool motivation and good behavior.

Fresh pots of Play-Doh are always useful, and this calendar has 24 of them, plus a new tool every day to go with each new color.

My car-fiend preschool kid would love this holiday-themed Hot Wheels Advent calendar. Each compartment is filled with either a 1:64-scale vehicle or a festive accessory for a vehicle, like reindeer antlers or a Santa hat.

My son and I are obsessed with Monster Jam’s blind-bag mini monster trucks because they are cute and surprisingly satisfying to push down a ramp or flexible race track — the wheels spin very fast! This Advent calendar variation will net you 16 mini monster trucks plus nine figures and accessories. Plus the packaging turns into a mud- and snow-filled arena with a 3-D cardboard jump so kids can re-create the fun of a real Monster Jam show.

If you’d rather add your own gifts and treats to an Advent calendar, this capacious Step2 gingerbread house is a great option for little kids. Each drawer is big enough for a small stuffy, an action figure, or a toy car.

Kids who love exploring Busytown will enjoy popping out a new scene each day to create Christmas ornaments for a tree, wreath, or garland. The calendar comes with gold thread for stringing each ornament.

Rather than having them open a new toy or treat each day, Melissa & Doug’s countdown calendar lets children add a new wooden ornament to their tree. Each one has a poem on the back that parents can read aloud.

Nostalgic parents like me who read the Little Miss and Mr. Men books as kids will love watching their kids open a wacky figurine or accessory each day.

Here’s one that’s perfect for Disney Princess–obsessed kids. The box transforms into a wintery castle with a cozy fireplace and foldout furniture, and you get three princesses, Tiana, Belle, and Rapunzel, plus accessories and animal friends for each.

You don’t actually have to be a fan of Jurassic Park to enjoy this Advent calendar. Any dinosaur-loving kid will appreciate the chance to open 19 miniature dinosaurs, one keeper, and four set pieces that together create the stage for tons of imaginative play.

The Wigglitz Advent calendar is mostly sold out online, but you can still find it at a couple of independent toy stores (just don’t dillydally). It comes with 24 holiday-themed creatures, one of which is extra special and shiny.

If you’ve got a kid who loves board games, especially Monopoly, this Advent calendar is full of holiday-themed Monopoly tokens to liven up the basic set — from a pink penguin to a gingerbread Monopoly Man — plus a bright red display to house them all.

Here’s an Advent calendar for your kid’s American Girl doll to open each day. It comes with 24 doll-size surprises, including sunglasses, hair accessories, a toy cell phone, snacks, and a purple beanie.

I like the idea of activity-based Advent calendars that won’t add toy clutter to a kid’s room. This one comes with 24 mini kawaii coloring books.

This Where’s Waldo calendar is also filled with mini-books, but instead of coloring, each one provides a different search-and-find challenge.

Each year, LEGO releases a handful of highly anticipated Advent calendars. My favorites of this year’s cohort are the LEGO Friends calendar set in a snowy ski chalet and the LEGO City calendar depicting Santa’s workshop.

While it’s not explicitly billed as an Advent calendar, this elaborate LEGO Christmas tree set comes with 24 bags of bricks inside the box, so families can chip away at the build as they count down to Christmas Day. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio and her family will be doing just that this year. Just be aware this set will likely sell out fast, so if you want to buy one, don’t wait.

Each section of this 25-day countdown to Christmas includes a holiday-themed mini-build with illustrated instructions.

This Magna-Tiles calendar has everything you need to build a Christmas train out of microMags. And the box folds out into a play set with train tracks.

Similarly, the PicassoTiles Advent calendar lets you build a festive gingerbread house.

Bluey fans will delight in opening a new figurine or accessory each day, including Bluey, Bingo, and Bartlebee as well as a buildable Christmas tree. Or if you’re looking for a little more razzle dazzle, there’s also a special Fuzzies edition that features flocked figurines.

Or you could get this Bluey jewelry Advent calendar with charms to build a bracelet and a necklace.

This New York City Ballet–themed keepsake box is my favorite of all the kids’ Advent calendars so far. Inside, you’ll find five paper characters from The Nutcracker to pose as you like. On top of that, the 24 compartments hold a gold-tone charm bracelet and an assortment of Nutcracker charms to go on it.

I also like this DIY-beaded-bracelet Advent calendar that’s much more affordable.

Here’s a putty-filled Advent calendar for anyone who can’t get their hands on the one from Aaron’s Crazy Thinking Putty.

Magic is a hobby that lends itself well to the Advent-calendar format. This National Geographic calendar comes with 24 magic tricks for kids to learn and the tools they need to pull them off.

Trolio’s two daughters have enjoyed this Thames & Kosmos calendar in past years. It contains all the materials kids need to do a new mini science experiment each day.

KiwiCo has multiple project-based Advent calendars, but this battery-powered winter wonderland for older kids is by far my favorite. It has a conveyor belt that helps sledders climb up a snowy hill, real working string lights, and an ice rink that shows skaters’ tracks.

Crafty kids get to make a dozen different cross-stitch ornaments with this Advent calendar.

For the many squishy hunters out there, this Squishmallows Advent calendar comes with 24 holiday Squish-a-longs that can each be worn as a ring.

Or here’s one for the Squishmallow traditionalists, with 24 mini winter- and holiday-themed Squishmallows, including a hilarious holiday ham.

You’ll get several “full-size” Fugglers, a few minis, and an assortment of stickers and other accessories in this 24-day Advent calendar devoted to the creepy yet kind of irrisistable creatures.

Inside this calendar, you’ll find ten Star Wars Bitty Pop vinyl figures, plus stackable cases and accessories to build your own Christmas-tree-shaped display.

This Pokémon Advent Calendar looks kind of like a coffee table book and opens to reveal a scene where kids can set up the pop-up tree, 24 days’ worth of ornaments featuring different Pokémon, and tree topper.

You’ll have to temper your expectations with this one: NeeDohs are still in great demand, and it’s extremely difficult to buy authentic ones online. If you are hoping to get a NeeDoh Advent calendar this year, your main strategy should be to haunt your local independent toy store and inquire often about availability and restocks. However, you can also keep an eye on the calendar at Amazon. Just don’t get your hopes up too high, as restocks are haphazard and available to to purchase by lottery only — if you get lucky and just so happen to refresh the product page at the right moment, you may be able to “request an invite” for a chance to buy the calendar at an unspecified future date.

Not technically an Advent calendar, but Taba Squishy is another popular squishy brand, and this case contains all 12 of this year’s holiday blind boxes, so you could start in mid-December and open one each day until Christmas.

Strategist writer Bella Druckman included this beauty-focused Advent calendar in her guide to the best Advent calendars for Gen Z because it feels curated by an actual teen. It’s got Starface pimple patches, a travel-size bodywash from Sol de Janeiro, and a mini version of the Billie Eilish perfume that topped wish lists last year.

Though it’s just ten days long, the Tonymoly x Squishmallows Advent calendar contains a nice mix of adorable and actually good bath and body products.

﻿Anthropologie’s embroidery Advent calendar also made Druckman’s list of good Advent calendars for Gen Z. Each day you embroider a new picture onto the calendar to fill out a holiday sampler over the course of a whole month.

Artsy tweens will appreciate the paint markers, mini-watercolors, travel paintbrush, and other arts and crafts in this city-shaped 24-day Advent calendar.

Another one for the crafty set, with materials to make a tiny roast turkey, gingerbread house, and more.

This slim Advent calendar comes with 12 days of darling Miffy sticker sheets.

Transport your kid to Tokyo with this extra-large 30-day Japan-themed Advent calendar featuring snacks, accessories, toys, stationery, and home goods.

Except for the first one, the doors on this Advent calendar aren’t numbered. Instead, each day, you must solve a new riddle, the solution to which will tell you which door to open next in an intergalactic race to celebrate Christmas.

Similar to the Exit calendar above, to solve the mystery at the end of this Clue-themed Advent calendar — and move on to the following day — you must solve riddles and crack codes behind each door. This is an excellent collaborative Advent calendar for families who love murder mysteries.

But if Dungeons & Dragons and other role-playing games are more your kid’s speed, this polar-bear-themed Advent calendar is full of festive dice that’ll make any gamer smile.

A Strategist favorite, the Bonne Maman Advent calendar contains 24 limited-edition spreads and jams to share and discuss each morning with family.

The Haribo Advent calendar is a real crowd-pleaser with a new pack of delicious gummies to open each day. You’ll just need to make a plan to deal with any sibling fights that erupt over the best ones.

In this ugly-sweater-themed Advent calendar, you get 25 different kinds of gourmet marshmallows. Each day is a surprise, with a clue to help you guess the flavor before opening.

For tween and teen baking enthusiasts, this calendar is full of cookie cutters, spatulas, piping bags, and more tools to make professional-grade holiday cookies.

This six-day calendar is a great intro to makeup for tweens and teens who love Snoopy. It comes with a freckle pen, highlighter stick, scented lip mask, scrunchie, compact mirror, and Snoopy plush keychain.
